I sought refuge in Allah from his anger, and he said, 'What is it with you and me? Whoever harms Ali has indeed harmed me.'" (Fada'il al-Sahaba, No. 1078)
Abu Bakr reported: "The Prophet (ﷺ) sent me with Bara'ah to the people of Makkah declaring that no polytheist would perform Hajj after that year, nor would anyone circumambulate the Kaaba naked, and only a Muslim soul shall enter Paradise. Whoever has a treaty with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), it shall be so until its final term. Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) are free from obligations to the polytheists. I traveled for 3 days, meanwhile, the Prophet (ﷺ) suddenly said to Ali, 'Catch up with Abu Bakr and take the message from him.' I returned to the Prophet (ﷺ) weeping, with fear in my heart I asked, 'O Messenger of Allah, did something happen?' The Prophet replied, 'Nothing concerning you but good. However, I was commanded by the Almighty that none but myself or a man from me should deliver it.'" (Musnad Ahmad, 1/3)
Indeed, the beauty of fear and awe of Allah manifested by Abu Bakr, the greatest among the Companions and the best of them, is profoundly touching. Abu Bakr, whose stature was elevated by Allah with numerous mentions in the Quran, wept out of fear of Allah, uncertain even if he had committed a sin or not. Truly, the greatness of this man is undeniable. Similarly, the glad tidings for Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, whom the Prophet (ﷺ) undoubtedly considered a son, a disciple, a son-in-law, and a great support, illustrate the deep and respected connections within the early Muslim community. Their lives, filled with devotion, humility, and a constant striving for righteousness, set a timeless example for all of us.
In another narration by Al-Baraa', may Allah be pleased with him, he said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) performed Umrah in Dhul-Qa'dah, the people of Makkah refused to allow him to enter it until they negotiated with him to stay there for 3 days. When they drafted the mutual agreement, Muslims wrote: 'This is what Muhammad the Messenger of Allah has agreed upon.' They said, 'We do not acknowledge you with this title. If we knew you were the Messenger of Allah, we would not have prevented you from anything, but you are Muhammad bin Abdullah.' The Prophet said, 'I am indeed, the Messenger of Allah and I am also Muhammad bin Abdullah.' Then he said to Ali, 'Erase "Messenger of Allah".' Ali said, 'By Allah The Great, I will never do that.' So, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took the document, although he could not write, and erase it himself leaving:
This is what Muhammad bin Abdullah has agreed upon:
He will not enter Makkah armed, except with a sword in its sheath, and no one from its (Makkah) people who wishes to follow him shall be allowed to join him, and none of his companions who wishes to stay or go back to it (Makkah) shall be prevented from doing so.'
When they entered it and the term expired, they came to Ali and said, 'Tell your cousin to leave the city, for the term has expired.' The Prophet (ﷺ) then left, and Hamza's daughter followed him, crying, 'O uncle, O uncle!' Ali took her by the hand and said to Fatimah, his wife, 'Take your cousin, carry her.' However, that raised a concern, for Ali, Zaid, and Ja'far disputed over her, each wanting to take care of her. Ali said, 'I will take her, for she is my cousin.' Ja'far said, 'Her aunt is my wife, and she is my cousin too.' Zaid said, 'She is my niece.' The Prophet (ﷺ) then decided she should be with her aunt and said, 'The aunt is of the same status as the mother.' He said to Ali, 'You are from me, and I am from you.' He said to Ja'far, 'You resemble me in my creation and character.' Finally, he said to Zaid, 'You are our brother and our freedman.' Ali, then, asked the Messenger (ﷺ), 'Why don't you marry Hamza’s daughter, the most beautiful and finest girl in Quraysh?' He said, 'O Ali, did you not know that Hamza is my brother through nursing, and Allah has forbidden in nursing what He has forbidden in lineage?' (Al-Bukhari, No. 4251)
The reflection on this story reveals the marvel of how the early Muslims interacted with one another. Observe how they were on the verge of contention over what? Over whom should take care of an orphan? In times when many of us scarcely remember offering charity to orphans, these individuals, despite their own preoccupations and limited means, were competing to take on more responsibility. Such determination and the beauty of their character and dignity are awe-inspiring.
Then, consider the approach of our great Prophet (ﷺ) in handling the situation. Although he chose one among the 3, given that the decision came from the Prophet (ﷺ), none could dispute it, which could have caused, albeit slightly, a wound in the hearts of the others, harboring it silently, yet, the healer of hearts (ﷺ), immediately proceeded to remind each one of their virtues, their closeness to him (ﷺ), and the love he held for each one in his heart. The absence of being chosen does not mean one is not up to the task, and the proof lies in how the Prophet (ﷺ) viewed each with such favorable traits. Thus, the disagreement was resolved, and everyone left content. Peace and blessings be upon him, truly a healer of hearts.
In regard to our story, and as a brief note, Hamza's daughter was named Umama. Ibn Ishaq narrated from Abdullah ibn Shaddad: "It was Salama ibn Abi Salama, who wed his mother, Umm Salama, to the Prophet (ﷺ). Later on, the Prophet (ﷺ) married Umama bint Hamza to him in name, for both were still young, and they did not come together until they died. The Prophet (ﷺ) then said, 'Have I not rewarded Salama?' Ibn Al-Kalbi said: 'It is said that Salama died before he could fully be with Umama.'" (Al-Isabah fi Tamyiz Al-Sahabah, No. 1995)
May God’s mercies, blessings, and forgiveness be upon this great pioneering generation of Muslims. Ameen.
CHAPTER 3:
Three Things More Valuable than the Whole World:
Sa'ad ibn Abi Waqqas reported: Muawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan ordered to meet me and said, "What prevents you from cursing Abu Turab (Ali)?"
Sa'ad replied, "Regarding 3 things I remember the Prophet (ﷺ) said about him, I will never curse him. For each of these to be mine would be dearer to me than the finest of red camels. First, the Prophet (ﷺ) left Ali behind in one of his battles, Ali said, 'O Messenger of Allah, you leave me with women and children?'
The Prophet said: 'Aren't you content, O Ali, to be to me as Aaron was to Moses, except that there is no prophet after me?'
The second, I heard him (ﷺ) on the day of Khaybar saying, 'I will give the banner [to a man] who loves Allah and His Messenger, and Allah and His Messenger love him.'
We were all hopeful for it, then he said, 'Call Ali for me.'
He was brought, his eyes sore, the Prophet (ﷺ) then spat into his eyes, handed him the banner, and Allah granted victory.
Third, when the verse came down: 'Come, let us call our sons and your sons.'
The Prophet called Ali, Fatimah, Hasan, and Husayn and said, 'O Allah, these are my family.'"
So, when Muawiyah heard all of that, he did not mention Ali with anything but good until he left Medina. (Muslim, No. 2404)
Ali, may Allah have mercy on his soul, he used to say:
Muhammad, the Prophet, my brother, my kin *** As Hamza, the lion, the martyr's crown he did win
Ja'far, who at dawn and dusk, does fly *** With angels, my brother, soaring high
Muhammad's daughter, my solace, my bride *** Her flesh intertwined with mine, side by side
From her, Ahmad's grandsons, my sons stand proud *** Who among you can claim a bond so loud?
To Islam, I rushed, in youth's early glow *** A boy not yet matured, in faith's fervent flow
I am the hero, known both in peace and in strife *** For days of despair and for days of life
The Prophet decreed, at Ghadir Khumm's stand *** My leadership over you, by his command
He chose me, by choice, for his allegiance so prime *** On the morrow, in mercy, through the passage of time
He entrusted to me, for his nation's decree *** So, who among you holds a station like me?
Woe, then woe, then woe again *** To those who deny my command, in vain. (Al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya, 9/8)
CHAPTER 4:
He Slept on the Prophet's Bed to Protect Him:
When the leaders of Quraysh realized that Muhammad (ﷺ), had gained followers and companions from outside their tribe and saw his companions migrating to join them, they understood that these followers had found a new stronghold and protection. They feared Muhammad's departure to his followers, knowing he was determined to wage war against them. So, they gathered in the Council Hall of Qusayy bin Kilab, called Daar Al-Nadwah, a place where Quraysh traditionally made their most crucial decisions, to discuss how to deal with Muhammad (ﷺ), now seen as a formidable threat.
Ibn Ishaq recounts, through reliable sources from Abdullah ibn Abbas and others, the story of that critical meeting. As Quraysh elite prepared to enter the Council Hall for their consultation, they encountered an old man of noble bearing at the doorway. This was none other than Satan himself, disguised as a sage from Najd, who had come to partake in their deliberation, offering his advice on their situation.
Standing at the doorway of the Council Hall, they inquired, "Who is this elder?" He replied, "A sage from the people of Najd, who heard of your assembly and has come to join you, hoping to offer counsel and advice." "Indeed, then enter," they welcomed him in. Inside, the elite of Quraysh had gathered: Utbah and Shaybah, Abu Sufyan, Taima ibn Adi, Jubayr ibn Mut'im ibn Adi, Al-Harith ibn Amir ibn Nawfal, Nadar ibn Al-Harith, Abu al-Bakhtari ibn Hisham, Zama'ah ibn Al- Aswad, Hakim ibn Hizam, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, Nabih and Munbih the sons of Al-Hajjaj, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and others from Quraysh, too numerous to count.
One among them, said to be Abu al-Bakhtari ibn Hisham, suggesting, "Let's imprison him in chains and lock him away. We'll wait for him to meet the same end as the poets before him, like Zuhayr and Al-Nabigha, who were forgotten by death. This way, he'll fade into obscurity just as they did." This proposal, among others, showed their willingness to go to great lengths to extinguish the prophetic light, not understanding that divine will cannot be obstructed by human schemes.
They said to one another, "This man has brought upon us what you have all witnessed. By Allah, we do not feel safe from him attacking us with those who have followed him from outside our tribe. Let's come to a unanimous decision regarding him."
After deliberating, one among them said to be Abu al-Bakhtari ibn Hisham, suggested, "Chain him in iron, lock the door upon him, and wait for him to meet the same fate as the poets before him, such as Zuhayr and Al-Nabigha, and those who have passed away from this death, until what befell them befalls him too." The elder from Najd sternly warned, "By Allah, this is not a wise counsel for you. If you imprison him as suggested, his message will still spread beyond these walls you've shut him behind to his followers. They are bound to storm your gates, snatch him from your grasp, and overwhelm you with their numbers until they dominate you entirely. This plan will not serve you well."
As they deliberated further, another among them proposed, "Let's exile him from our midst, sending him away from our land. Once he's gone, we care not where he ends up. His absence will ease our affairs and restore our unity as before." The elder from Najd countered again, "By Allah, this too is folly. Have you not witnessed his eloquent speech and the sweetness of his discourse? His ability to captivate men's hearts with his words? Should you do this, I fear he might settle among any tribe of the Arabs, win them over with his speech, and then lead an army against you, seizing control and doing with you as he pleases. Consider another course of action."
It was Abu Hakam ibn Hisham (a.k.a., Abu Jahl) who then declared, "By Allah, I have a plan none of you have yet considered." They asked, "What is it, O Abu Al- Hakam?" He said, "We should select a strong, noble youth from each tribe and arm each one with a sharp sword. Then, they should strike him simultaneously, ensuring his death. This way, we'd be rid of him, and his blood would be on all our hands, making it impossible for Banu Abd Manaf to seek vengeance against all tribes. They'd be forced to accept blood money, which we would gladly pay." The elder from Najd agreed, "What this man proposes is the only viable plan. There's no alternative." The group then dispersed, united on this plan. Jibril, may God be pleased with him, then came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and instructed him, "Do not sleep on your bed tonight where you usually do."
As night fell, the assassins gathered at his door, waiting for him to sleep so they could attack. The Prophet (ﷺ), seeing their position, asked Ali bin Abi Talib to sleep on his bed and cover himself with his green Hadrami cloak, assuring Ali that no harm from the assassins would reach him. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to sleep in that cloak when he slept. On his way out, he recited:
{
Yaa Sin. By the wise Qur'an, Lo! thou art of those sent. On a straight path, a revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful, that thou mayst warn a folk whose fathers were not warned, so they are heedless. Already hath the judgment, (for their infidelity) proved true of most of them, for they believe not. Lo! We have put on their necks carcans reaching unto the chins, so that they are made stiff-necked. And We have set a bar before them and a bar behind them, and (thus) have covered them so that they see not. Whether thou warn them or thou warn them not, it is alike for them, for they believe not. Thou warnest only him who followeth the Reminder and feareth the Beneficent in secret. To him bear tidings of forgiveness and a rich reward.
}
(Quran, 36:1-19), and had placed dust upon all the assassins’ heads. Then, he left towards his intended destination.
Someone who was not among them came and asked, "What are you waiting for here?" They said, "Muhammad." He said, "May God disappoint you, for indeed, by God, Muhammad has come out upon you, not leaving a single man among you without putting dust on his head, and he has gone on his way. Do you not see what has become of you?"
Every man among them placed his hand upon his head, and what a surprise, it was covered in dust. They started looking around and saw someone on the bed, wrapped in the Prophet Muhammad's cloak, and they said, "By God, this is Muhammad sleeping in his cloak." They remained in that state until dawn when Ali got up from the bed. They said, "By God, it turned out as we had been told." (Al-Seerah Al-Nabawiyah, 2/228-230)
The valiant "Haydar" (i.e., a name given to Ali ibn Abi Talib by his mother) protected the mission in the person of its Prophet (ﷺ) and slept in his bed on the most perilous night the mission had ever faced. A man slept in the bed knowing that at the door were men who wanted nothing but the head of the one sleeping on that bed. What a sacrifice! What a bravery!
Therefore, when he was troubled for one night at that bed for the sake of his Prophet (ﷺ), God blessed his bed with Fatimah, the daughter of his Prophet (ﷺ), who manifested in her perfection for his sake. The Messenger (ﷺ) himself was, once again, his welcoming family, and his dowry was his own shield, presented to him with a wool-stuffed leather pillow, a water skin, a sieve, a wooden cup, a hand mill, two sacks, and she entered his life with no bed but the skin of a ram they slept on at night and which was used to feed their camel during the day. She was her own servant. By God, such a thing did not detract from her high position.
Ibn Abi Layla narrated: "Ali told us that Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her, complained about the effect of the hand mill. When captives were brought to the Prophet (ﷺ), she went to him to ask for a servant. She didn't find him but informed Aisha. When the Prophet (ﷺ) came, Aisha told him about Fatimah's visit. The Prophet came to us after we had gone to bed. I was about to rise, but he said, 'Stay where you are.' He sat down between us until I felt the coolness of his feet on my chest and said, 'Shall I not teach you something better than what you asked of me? When you go to bed, glorify Allah 34 times (Takbir), praise Him 33 times (Tasbeeh), and magnify Him 33 times (Ham’d), for that is better for you than a servant." (Al-Bukhari, No. 3705)
In another narration, narrated by Umm Salamah, Mother of the Believers: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called for Fatimah in the Year of the Conquest of Makkah to speak to her, and she cried. Then he spoke to her, and she laughed. She said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died I asked her about her crying and her laughing. She said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informed me that he would, soon die, so I cried. Then, he informed me that I was the master over all of the women among the inhabitants of Paradise, except for Mariam bint Imran [i.e., Mary, The Virgin, Mother of Jesus (ﷺ)], so I laughed.'" (Al-Tirmidhi, No. 3893)
He (ﷺ) used to say, "Fatimah is a part of me, whoever angers her angers me." (Al-Bukhari, No. 3767)
Anas, may God be pleased with him, reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, Paradise longs for three: Ali, Ammar, and Salman" (Sahih al-Jami, No. 1598). What a splendid reward, indeed!
CHAPTER 5:
His Struggle in the Path of Allah:
Indeed, he, may Allah be pleased with him, inscribed upon the forehead of history with lines of light, bright pages from his struggle in the path of Allah Almighty. He sought martyrdom and longed for it with the longing of one searching for cool water in a desolate desert.
Ibn Hajar, the distinguished Hafiz, tells us that: “The virtues of Ali are so numerous that Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal did not transmit for anyone among the Companions what he transmitted for Ali in terms of merits.” (Al-Isabah, 2/501)
This should hardly surprise us, for Ali was a personification of the prophetic nurturing; he was a conduit that overflowed with all the goodness that emanated from it. Echoing this sentiment, the great Andalusian jurist, Hafiz Ibn Abd al-Barr, also states: "The virtues of Ali cannot be encompassed by a book." (Al-Istiiab, 2/833)
However, the crowning jewel in the vast array of virtues that no book can fully capture about this righteous Caliph is his immense contribution to the jihad in the path of Allah and elevating the banner of Islam and Muslims. From his youth until he aged and passed away, he lived his entire life defending the religion of Allah, the honor of Muslims, and the strength of Islam. In this book, it would not be possible to enumerate all the battles and wars he participated in, but we will highlight the most prominent ones for the reader:
CHAPTER 6:
His Jihad on the Day of Badr:
In the Battle of Badr, Ali the valiant warrior went out, fighting in the way of Allah. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: "On the day of Badr, three partners were sharing a camel: Abu Lubaba and Ali ibn Abi Talib and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It was the turn of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to walk. They said: We will walk instead of you. He said: ‘You are not stronger than me, nor do I need the reward less than you.’" (Musnad Ahmad 1/411)
Indeed, in the land of honor and jihad, where tongues are silent and swords speak above the heads, our hero had this magnificent stance. Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib, himself, recounts the critical espionage role he played before the battle. He had brought back vital intelligence about Quraysh army's strength to the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), which would be pivotal in the Muslims' strategic preparations.
Harithah ibn Mudrib narrates from Ali, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was gathering intelligence about Quraysh army near Badr. When word reached us that Qurayshis were approaching, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) marched towards Badr’s well. We outpaced Quraysh to it and found two men there, one from Quraysh and a slave of Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt.
The Qurayshi managed to escape, but we captured Uqba's slave. When we asked him about the size of the enemy forces, he kept saying, 'By Allah, they are numerous and formidable.' Each time he said this, the Muslims struck him until they brought him before the Prophet (ﷺ), who then asked, 'How many are they, exactly?'
The man repeated, 'By Allah, they are numerous and formidable.' The Prophet tried to extract an exact number from him, but he refused to say.
Then, cleverly, the Prophet (ﷺ) inquired, 'How many camels do they slaughter each day?'
He replied, 'About 10.'
The Prophet (ﷺ) deduced, 'The enemy numbers 1000, each camel for 100 men.'
That night, we were hit by a sudden shower of rain. We sought shelter under trees and in the lee of rocks to escape the downpour. The Prophet (ﷺ) spent the night beseeching his Lord, imploring, 'O Allah, if this group perishes, You will not be worshipped again.' As dawn broke, the call was made, 'Prayer, O servants of Allah.' People emerged from their shelters to join the Prophet (ﷺ) in prayer, after which he rallied them for battle, pointing out, 'Quraysh gather beneath that red hill by the mountain.' As the enemy drew closer and we faced them in ranks, a man on a red camel moved among Quraysh ranks. The Prophet (ﷺ) said, 'Ali, call Hamza.' He was the closest to the pagans, and he knew the majority of them. 'Who is the man on the red camel? What is he saying to them?' The Prophet (ﷺ) then remarked, 'If there is anyone among the enemy who advocates for goodness, it might well be the man on the red camel.'
Hamza returned and reported, 'He is Utbah ibn Rabiah, dissuading from battle, saying to them: "O people! I see a determined foe you cannot reach without sacrifice. If need be, let today's censure fall upon me, say 'Utbah ibn Rabiah has turned coward,' though you know I am not the most cowardly among you."' Upon hearing this, Abu Jahl rebuked, 'Do you say this? By Allah, if another said so, I would have reproached him severely. You've filled your heart and chest with fear.' Utbah retorted, 'You reproach me, O you fool? You will know today who the coward is.'
So, he (Utbah ibn Rabi'ah) stepped forward, followed by his son and his brother, and called out: Who will duel us? Young men from the Ansar volunteered, but he said: “Who are you? I don’t recognize any of you.” When they informed him, he said: “We have no need of you; we wanted our cousins for the duel.”
The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: “Stand up, O Hamza, stand up, O Ali, stand up, O Ubaydah ibn al-Harith.” Hamza went forth to Utbah, and I went to Shaybah, and a duel ensued between Ubaydah and Walid where each wounded his opponent, then we leaned towards Walid, killed him, and carried Ubaydah away." (Sunan Abu Dawud, No. 2665) (Al-Musannaf, 8/469)
From Qais bin Ubad that: Ali bin Abi Talib said, "I shall be the first man to kneel down before (Allah), the Beneficent to receive His judgment on the day of Resurrection (in my favor)."
Qais bin Ubad also said, "The following Ayah was revealed in their connection:"
{
These twain (the believers and the disbelievers) are two opponents who contend concerning their Lord. But as for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them; boiling fluid will be poured down on their heads.
}
(Quran, 22:19)
Qais said that they were those who fought on the day of Badr, namely, Hamza, Ali, Abu 'Ubaida bin Al-Harith, Shaiba bin Rabi`a, Utba and Al-Wahd bin Utba. (Al-Bukhari, No. 3965)
CHAPTER 7:
His Jihad on the Day of Al-Khandaq:
During the Battle of Al-Khandaq, he had this magnificent stance against the well- known warrior of Quraysh, Amr ibn Abd Wud al-Amiri. Amr al-Amiri, or “The Vanguard of the Battalion”, as he was known, had attended the great battle of Badr and tasted the bitterness of defeat after being wounded in the battle. He vowed not to oil his head until he killed Muhammad (ﷺ). Thus, he was among the first horsemen to storm the trench towards the Muslims, accompanied by warriors from Quraysh. Ali ibn Abi Talib, along with a group of Muslims, went forth until they secured the breach through which their horses had charged, and the horsemen hastened towards them.
Ibn Ishaq said: "Amr ibn Abd Wud al-Amiri, The Vanguard of the Battalion, had fought on the day of Badr and had deep injuries that detained him from joining Uhud. On the day of Al-Khandaq, he emerged to survey the scene, and when he and his horsemen stood, clad in iron armor, came out and shouted: 'Who will duel?' Ali ibn Abi Talib stood up and said: 'I am ready, O Prophet of Allah.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'It is Amr, sit down.'
Then, Amr called out again: 'Isn't there a man to duel? He rebuked them saying: 'Where is your paradise which you claim that one who is killed from among you will enter? Why won't you come out to duel a single man like me?' Ali stood up again and said: 'I am ready, O Messenger of Allah, allow me to face him.' The Prophet said: 'Sit down.' When he called out for the third time, saying:
My voice has grown hoarse from the call *** "Is there any challenger, any at all?"
I stood firm when the encouragers fled *** Like a horn ready to clash, my resolve spread
I have always rushed before the wars begin *** For bravery in a youth, and generosity, are virtues akin.
Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, stood up again and said: "O Messenger of Allah, it is I." The Prophet said: "It is Amr." Ali replied: "Even if it is Amr, I do not care." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then gave him permission, and he walked towards him, reciting:
Do not hasten, for your call has been met *** By one who responds, without regret
With intention and insight *** Truth is the savior of every right
I hope to leave upon you a mark so dire *** A lament of funerals, your requiem choir
From a sword's strike, its memory will last *** In the annals of war, forever cast.
When Ali approached Amr to duel him, he said: "O Amr, you used to claim that you would not refuse if someone proposed one of 3 options to you." Amr said: "Indeed." Ali then said: "I invite you to bear witness that there is no god, but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and to submit to the Lord of the worlds." Amr replied: "O nephew, spare me this." Ali offered a second option: "Return to your land, for if Muhammad is indeed the Messenger of Allah, you would be the happiest of people with him, and if he is lying, then you get what you desire." Amr said: "This is not something the women of Quraysh will ever speak of. How can I forsake my vow when I am able to fulfill it?!"
Amr then asked: "What is the third option?" Ali replied: "To duel." The warrior of Quraysh, Amr, who was a renowned aged knight, laughed hard and said to Ali: "This quality, I never thought any Arab would dare challenge me with." Then, Amr asked Ali: "Who are you?" Ali responded: "I am Ali." Amr asked: "Are you the son of Abd Manaf?" Ali said: "I am Ali ibn Abi Talib." Amr said: "O nephew, is there among your uncles anyone older than you? By God, I do not wish to kill you." Ali replied: "But I, by Allah, wish to kill you."
At that point, Amr became furiously angry, descended, unsheathed his sword, shining like a flame, and then advanced towards Ali in rage. Ali faced him with his shield; Amr struck at Ali's shield, missing him, and the sword stuck in the shield, hitting his head and causing a wound. Ali, then, struck Amr on the neck, causing him to fall, and dust rose. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard the Takbir, so it was known among the people that Ali had killed Amr. Then, Ali said:
Do warriors charge thus fiercely, I hear *** From me, and of them, my fellows bear fear?
Today, my honor flight does repeal *** In my soul, a resolve, stronger than steel
Upon seeing Amr's defeat, Akrimah threw his spear, and Hassan ibn Thabit remarked with a jeer:
You fled, casting your spear to us, in fear *** Perhaps, Akrimah, such acts you did not endear
You turned to run as if pursued by shadows dark *** Not veering from justice, not missing the mark
Your back, not comforted by the fray's spark *** Became like the backs of hyenas, stark.
Umar bin Al-Khattab said to Ali: "Why didn't you strip his armor off, referring to Amr bin Abd Wudd, for there is not a better armor among the Arabs than his?" Ali replied: "I struck him down, and he exposed his private parts, so I felt ashamed to strip him." The polytheists sent to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), offering 10000 coins to buy his corpse. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Give them his corpse, for it is vile, and so is its price." He accepted nothing from them. (Al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya, 4/106)
CHAPTER 8:
The Standard-Bearer Who Allah Granted Victory Through on the Day of Khaybar:
During the historic battle of Khaybar, the Prophet (ﷺ) bore witness to Ali, may Allah bestow His pleasure upon him, that he holds a profound love for Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ), and in turn, is dearly loved by Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ), also is through Ali that Allah will bestow victory that day.
Sahl bin Sa'ad, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), said on the day of Khaybar: "I will give this flag tomorrow to a man through whom Allah will grant victory, who loves Allah and His Messenger, and is loved by Allah and His Messenger." The people spent their night in wonder as to whom it would be given. In the morning, they all hoped to receive it. The Prophet (ﷺ) asked: "Where is Ali bin Abi Talib?" It was said, "He is suffering from an eye ailment, O Messenger of Allah." They sent for him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) spat in his eyes, prayed for him, and he was healed as if he had no ailment. The Prophet (ﷺ) then gave him the flag.
Ali asked, "O Messenger of Allah, shall I fight them until they become like us?" The Prophet (ﷺ) replied: "Proceed calmly until you enter their territory, then invite them to Islam and inform them of their duties to Allah. By Allah, if Allah guides a man through you, it is better for you than red camels. (Al-Bukhari, No. 4210).
In another narration, Abu Huraira reported that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said on the day of Khaybar: "I will indeed give this flag to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger, and through whom Allah will grant victory." Umar bin Al- Khattab said: "I never longed for leadership except on that day. I, actually, hoped to be called for it. However, The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called Ali bin Abi Talib and gave it to him, saying, "Go, and do not turn back until Allah grants you victory." Ali proceeded a bit, then stopped without turning back, and yelled, "O Messenger of Allah, on what basis do I fight the people?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Fight them until they testify there is no deity except Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. If they do that, they have protected from you their blood and wealth, except by its right, and their account is with Allah (Muslim, No. 2405)."
Salama also reported that: "Ali couldn’t follow the Prophet (ﷺ) to Khaybar’s battlefield because he had conjunctivitis. He said, 'How can I stay behind the Prophet of Allah?' So, he set out and joined the Prophet (ﷺ). On the evening preceding the morning Allah granted us victory, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Tomorrow I will give the flag, or he said the standard, to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger, or he said: whom Allah and His Messenger love, and Allah will grant victory through him.' Suddenly, we saw Ali coming, and we had not been expecting him at all. They said: 'This is Ali.' So, the Prophet (ﷺ) gave him the flag, and Allah granted victory through him" (Al-Bukhari, No. 3702).
Abu Sa'id al-Khudri reported: "The Messenger of Allah shook the flag then said, 'Who will take it rightfully?' A man came forward saying, 'I will.' He said, 'Sit down.' Then another man came forward, and he said, 'Sit down.' Then he said, 'By the One who honored Muhammad’s face, I will give it to a man who does not flee. Here, take it, Ali. Go forth until Allah grants you victory.” So, he went over Khaybar and Fadak, bringing back their dates and dry meat.'" (Al-Musnad, 3/16).
During that campaign, "Marhab," a formidable Jewish warrior, came forth saying:
Khaybar has known, I am Marhab, *** A warrior tried, in armor clad
When wars ignite their furious flame *** I'm the tempest that no shield can tame.
Ali replied:
I am the one my mother named Hydara *** Like a lion of the forests, daunting in aura
To foes, I give measure for measure *** With the full weight of a storm's pressure
Marhab was a knight among the Jews, inscribed on his sword in Hebrew was: This is the sword of Marhab *** Whose taste leaves foes on their slab
A bitter draught of the end's whisper *** For those who meet it, no morning's glimmer
Hence, Ali struck him, severing his helmet, and his head, up to his molars. (Muslim, No. 1807)
Before this, Ali had killed Marhab's brother, Al-Harith, and faced another Jewish leader, called Amer. The Prophet (ﷺ), upon seeing this man emerge, remarked in surprise, "Is he five cubits (i.e., 90 inches) tall?" He was indeed tall and imposing. When called to a duel, and he brandished his sword, armored and helmeted, shouting for a challenger, the people hesitated. Ali stepped forward, striking him repeatedly without effect, until he hit his legs, bringing him down, then finishing him off and taking his arms. And thus, Allah granted victory through Ali over the fortress of Na'im, one of Khaybar's strongest. Such illustrious pages of history we shall never forget as long as we live. (Silsilat Ma’arik Al-Islam Al-Fasilah, 122)
CHAPTER 9:
Treaty of Hudaybiyyah:
During the expedition of Hudaybiyyah, prior to the treaty, some Muslim slaves from Makkah fled to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Their masters wrote to him (ﷺ), requesting their return, but the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) refused to send them back and said, "O people of Quraysh, desist, or Allah will send someone against you who will strike your necks with the sword for the sake of the religion. Allah has tested his heart for faith." The Companions eagerly asked, "Who is he, O Messenger of Allah?" hoping each to be the one commended by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He replied, "The one mending the sandal," and it was Ali who was mending it for the Prophet (ﷺ).
Afterwards, Quraysh violated their treaty with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by supporting the clan of Banu Bakr against Khuza'ah, the allies of the Muslims, and aided them with men and arms. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) declared, "Help is granted, O Amr ibn Salim. Allah has not helped me if I do not help the sons of Ka'b." And upon seeing clouds in the sky, he said, "This cloud heralds victory for the sons of Ka'b."
Amr ibn Salim, head of Khuza'ah clan, came to Medina and recited a poem in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), part of which stated:
O Lord, I call upon Muhammad's bond *** The pact between our fathers, and beyond
You were once the children, and we the parent to you *** Then we embraced Islam, steadfast and true
Grant, O Allah, support that's just and strong *** Summon Your servants, to aid and belong
Among them, Allah's Messenger, stands pure *** Sees injustice, his visage shows his fury sure
In an army vast as the sea, foaming, unbound *** For Quraysh broke the promise they had found
They shattered the covenant, firm and deep *** Set traps for me, their watch to keep
Claiming I call not to anyone's aid *** Yet for we are fewer, in humiliation laid
They slept in our house, under night’s cover *** Killed us in prayer, no mercy to discover
Meanwhile, Quraysh sent Abu Sufyan, one of their elites, to Medina to affirm the peace and extend its term. Upon reaching the city and presenting his case to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the Prophet (ﷺ) turned away, not responding. Abu Sufyan sought the intercession of senior Sahabah like Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali to mediate between him and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but all refused. Thus, Abu Sufyan returned to Makkah without securing any agreement or pledge. (Al-Tareekh Al-Siyasi Wa Al-Askari, 365)
CHAPTER 10:
Thwarting a Spy Effort for Quraysh:
Narrated by Ubaydullah ibn Abi Rafi', he said: He heard Ali say, "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent me, along with Al-Zubair and Al-Miqdad, and said, 'Go until you reach the garden of Khakh; there, you will find a woman with a letter. Take it from her.'" We spurred our horses until we reached the garden and found the woman. We said, "Give us the letter." She denied having anyone. We said, "You will either give us the letter or we will do the necessary measurements to take it from you." She then took out the letter from her hair and we brought it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Surprisingly, it was from Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, one of the companions, to some polytheists in Makkah, informing them of some of the Messenger's plans (ﷺ).
The Messenger (ﷺ) summoned Hatib and asked, "What is this?" Hatib pleaded, "Do not hasten to judge me. I was an outsider in Quraysh, not one of their blood, whereas those who are with you from the Muhajirin have relatives in Makkah who protect their families. I wished to make a connection in Makkah to protect mine, not out of disbelief, apostasy, or satisfaction with disbelief after Islam." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "He has told you the truth." Angrily, Umar said, "Let me strike the neck of this hypocrite." But the Prophet said, "He has witnessed Badr, and fought for the sake of Allah. How do you know, O Umar? Perhaps Allah has looked upon the people of Badr and said, 'Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you.'" (Musnad Ahmad, No. 600)
In another significant incident involving Umm Hani bint Abi Talib, Ali's sister: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived at the higher part of Makkah during the conquest of the city, 2 of my relatives from Banu Makhzum sought refuge with me, including Hubayrah ibn Abi Wahb al-Makhzumi. Ali, my brother, entered the house, found them, and then swore by Allah to kill them both without hesitation. I locked them in a room, then went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who was at the upper part of Makkah. I found him bathing in a trough that still had some dough traces on it (for it was used for cooking), while his daughter Fatimah screened him with a garment. After his bath, he donned his clothes and prayed 8 rak’at for the Duha prayer. He then turned to me and said, 'Welcome, Umm Hani, what brings you here?' Therefore, I informed him about the 2 men of my relatives and Ali's intent, to which he declared, 'We grant protection to those you have protected, Umm Hani, and do ensure safety to those you have ensured; they shall not be killed.'" (Sahih Al-Sirah, 527)
This incident exemplifies that a Muslim's assurance of safety to a non-believer from a hostile party grants them protection, thus, other Muslims are forbidden from harming them. To preserve the integrity of this protection and prevent any harm to Muslims as a consequence, jurists have stipulated that the one offering protection should be free from suspicion, the assurance should be devoid of any harm, or the matter should be referred to the ruler for his decision.
Another point is that; while reflecting on the poignant tale of Umm Hani's, we are reminded, one more time, of the esteemed position that women held in the early Islamic Ummah. This story not only underscores the Prophet's (ﷺ) merciful nature but also highlights the profound respect and consideration he accorded to the opinions and actions of women. Umm Hani's ability to protect and advocate for the lives of her relatives, in the first place, hiding them, challenging his brother, may Allah be pleased with him, who was one of the most influential figures at that time, and the Prophet's immediate affirmation of her decision, exemplify the integral role women played in shaping the moral and social fabric of their time. Through this narrative, we glean the timeless lesson that wisdom, compassion, and the pursuit of justice transcend gender, affirming the dignity and respect owed to every individual's voice and actions in Islam.
And thus came the grand day of the full Conquest, when Makkah, finally shedding the dust of polytheism sullied by the idolaters, adorned the garment of Islam for eternity. The Prophet (ﷺ) had instructed his commanders to fight only those who fought them. However, he specifically named individuals whose blood was forfeited, even if they were found beneath the drapes of the Kaaba, including Al-Huwayrith ibn Naqidh ibn Wahb. He had harassed the Prophet (ﷺ) in Makkah and, during the Hijrah, when Al-Abbas escorted the Prophet's daughters, Fatimah and Umm-Kulthum, may Allah be pleased with them both, to Medina, Al-Huwayrith attacked their camel, causing them to fall and be injured. Hence, the Prophet (ﷺ) decreed his blood permissible, and Ali killed him on that day. (Seerat Ibn Hisham, 4/58-59)
CHAPTER 11:
An Envoy and Messenger of Peace:
After the Conquest, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Ali to the clan of Banu Jadhima to rectify the mistake made by Khalid bin Al-Walid in killing some of them. After the conquest of Makkah in the 8th year of Hijrah, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had dispatched Khalid to Banu Jadhima to invite them to Islam. However, they did not correctly articulate their acceptance of Islam and instead said, "Sab'ana!" (i.e., “We have left the religion”, meaning their previous religion not Islam), leading Khalid to misunderstand their statement and kill and capture some of them. When the news of Khalid's actions reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he raised his hands and said, "O Allah, I absolve myself before You of what Khalid has done," twice. (Al-Bukhari, No. 4339)
Thus, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Ali to look into their matter, providing him with enough resources for this task. Ali fulfilled his duty excellently, compensating them for the bloodshed and loss of property, even to the extent of indemnifying the value of a dog's bowl. After completing these compensations, he asked them, "Is there any claim of blood or property that has not been compensated to you?" They replied, "No." He said, "I give you this remaining money as a precautionary measure from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for what neither you nor we may know." He did so, and upon his return to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informing him of the actions taken, he, relievedly said, "You did really well and acted rightly." (Seerat Ibn Hisham, 4/72-73)
Through this noble and successful mission, Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, alleviated a concern and burden that weighed heavily on the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). With this wise prophetic guidance, he consoled Banu Jadhima, removing any grief and sorrow from their hearts. It also should be noted that Khalid's killing of some people from Banu Jadhima was a misjudgment and misinterpretation on his part, evidenced by the fact that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) neither punished him for his actions nor dismissed him from his position.
CHAPTER 12:
Ali in the Battle of Hunayn:
The conquest of Makkah instilled fear and terror in the hearts of the polytheists, causing panic among them. The tribes of Ta'if, primarily Hawazin and Thaqif, along with other tribes, resolved to quickly confront the Muslim army before it could turn on them. They assembled a vast army led by a valiant and courageous young man named Malik ibn Auf al-Nasri, and they marched towards the Muslims. (Seerat Ibn Hisham, 4/80)
The Prophet (ﷺ) promptly decided to face them at the head of a formidable army consisting of 12000 men; 10000 from Medina and 2000 newly converted Muslims of Makkah. The enormity of the army led some to overconfidence, to the point where it was said: "We cannot be defeated today due to lack of numbers." (Al-Tabaqat, 2/150)
Malik ordered his army to hide behind big stones, rocks, and the crevices of mountains, and at high points at the end of the valley, which was a passage to the area of Hunayn. When the Islamic army reached there, they were ambushed with arrows and stones, suffering defeat and disarray, leading many from the Prophet’s army to flee. (Al-Kamil Fi Al-Tareekh, 1/625).
It was disastrous, to the point where Abu Sufyan, one of those whose hearts had been recently reconciled towards Islam, mockingly said: "Their defeat will not end until they reach the sea." (Tarikh Al-Islam, 2/576).
In this moment of adversity, only a few remained with the Prophet (ﷺ), about 10, as he fought saying: "I am the Prophet, truly spoken, from Abdul Muttalib's lineage, unbroken." Only a small group of the Prophet's Sahabah, those who were the earliest in embracing Islam and known for their valor, steadfastness, and bravery, stayed with him. Among them were Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq, Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, Al-Abbas, his son Fadl, Abu Sufyan ibn Harith, Usama ibn Zaid and others who quickly returned to the battle and were counted among those who did not flee. Of course, among those who stood firm and defended the Prophet (ﷺ) with their sword and life was Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. He tirelessly defended the Prophet (ﷺ), driving back those who sought to kill him and forcing them to retreat. (Seerat Ibn Hisham, 4/85)
In the midst of these adversities and challenges, the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) raised his voice loudly, calling out: "O supporters of Allah and His Messenger, I am the servant of Allah and am His messenger!" However, his voice was not heard by the people, as he was not loud by nature. He then requested his uncle Al-Abbas, known for his booming voice, to call out to the people, which he quickly did: "O assembly of the Ansar, O assembly of the Samurah (i.e., name of the tree where the Pledge of Al-Ridwan took place)!"
They responded: "At your service, at your service." A man would try to turn his camel around but couldn't, so he would grab his shield, throw it over his shoulders, take his sword, and dismount his camel to make his way towards the voice, eventually reaching the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). Once about 100 of them had gathered around him, they faced the enemy more effectively, and thus the order of the army was reformed, and they fought until victory was theirs. (Tarikh Al-Rusul Wa Al-Muluk, 3/75)
However, Ali's steadfastness and relentless fighting in this particular battle are also noteworthy; he killed 40 men from Hawazin, including Abu Jerwal, one of their bravest, for he was a strong fighter on a red camel holding a black banner, who would strike with his spear when he could reach the Muslims, and when people fell behind, he lifted his spear so those behind him could follow. Ali, with his military acumen and extensive experience, realized that this man played a significant role in the morale and fierceness of Hawazin. So, he, may Allah be pleased with him, and another man from Al-Ansar headed towards him directly and managed to dismount and kill him. His death marked the beginning of their army's collapse, leading to the enemy's defeat and the Muslims' victory within an hour. (Musnad Abu Ya'la, modified, 3/388)
Jabir ibn Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with him, described this incident with more details saying: "As the bearer of the Hawazin standard rode his red camel, doing what he did, Ali ibn Abi Talib, and a man from the Ansar aimed for him. Ali approached from behind, striking the camel's hock, causing it to fall, while the Ansari leapt onto the man, delivering a blow that severed his foot at the shin, tumbling him from his saddle. The battle intensified, and by Allah, the retreat did not cease until they found prisoners already bound in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." (Seerat Ibn Hisham, 2/446)
This situation offers several lessons for the proponents of truth and its soldiers to ponder for a long time. The defeat of a cause in a battle might stem from the weakening of some of its members' faith, their lack of dedication to the truth, and their unpreparedness to sacrifice for it. The steadfastness of the cause's leader (ﷺ) during crises, his courage, and his trust in Allah's support significantly contribute to turning defeat into victory, strengthening the hearts of the weak and hesitant among his followers.
The sincere and steadfast supporters of truth rallying around their bold and dedicated leader also play a significant role in converting defeat into victory. Those who remained with the Prophet (ﷺ) after the initial defeat in the battle and those who heeded his call did not exceed 100 men. At that point, the tide of the battle began to turn, marking the beginning of Allah's support for His faithful servants, the weakening of His enemies, and the onset of discord within their ranks and hearts. As the leader of the cause and his soldiers remember that they are on the side of truth and that Allah is with the truthful believers, their morale strengthens, and their willingness to sacrifice and persevere increases.
Consider also, the Prophet's (ﷺ) leading, and communication skills in his declaration: "I am the Prophet, truly spoken, from Abdul Muttalib's lineage, unbroken," which stands as a testament to the truthfulness of his claim to prophethood and his confidence in the support of his Lord.
Thus, a leader should always, especially in times of hardship, be confident, seek refuge in his Lord, and be assured of His victory and care. The leader's confidence in his mission and purpose has the greatest impact on his success, rallying people around him, and it significantly eases the burden of hardships, allowing him to endure pain with contentment and peace. (Al-Seerah Al-Nabawiyah, 1/140)
Since we are discussing some aspects of this grand epic even detailed in the Book of Allah, and as we've discussed the profound influence of Muslim women in the early Muslim communities earlier, we turn our attention to another remarkable woman, Umm Sulaim bint Milhan. She presented a glorious example of Muslim women's valor in the dawn of Islam. Umm Sulaim participated in this battle alongside her noble companion husband, Abu Talha Al-Ansari [different from Talha Ibn Abd Allah]. Armed with determination, a sword by her side, and pregnant, she also was managing a camel for Abu Talha, fearing it might escape.
She ingeniously tied her hand with its nose ring and lead, securing this huge animal on the battlefield and in a very critical situation like that which proved nothing but amazing determination and power of mind. The Prophet (ﷺ) noticed her, so, he inquired, "Umm Sulaim, what brings you here?"
She declared, "By my father and mother, O Messenger of Allah! Do not be lenient with those who flee and desert you; rather, please fight them just like you fight our enemy here, for they are indeed deserving."
The Prophet (ﷺ) replied, with his usual merciful words even in such an “hour of difficulty” as the Quran describes it, he said, "May Allah suffice me the harm, O Umm Sulaim!"
Noticing she carried a dagger, her husband, Abu Talha, asked about its purpose. She said, "I have taken it so that if any of the disbelievers approach me, I will rip him apart with it!" Abu Talha was impressed by her courage and strength, and turning towards the Prophet (ﷺ), he smiled and proudly said, "Do you hear what Umm Sulaim says, O Messenger of Allah? Do you hear it?"
Thus was the Muslim woman: bold, participating directly in battles, ready to defend herself against enemies to avoid capture, embodying the radiant pages of sacrifice, bravery, and dedication in the early history of Islam.
CHAPTER 13:
Ali's Campaign to Demolish the Idol of Fals:
After the Prophet (ﷺ) had purified the Kaaba from the idols within it, it became necessary to demolish the idols that had long been landmarks of ignorance. Thus, the campaigns of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) followed one after another to cleanse the peninsula of them. It fell upon Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, to destroy the idol of Fals in the lands of Tai'. In the spring of that year, a force led by him set out to demolish Fals, an idol of Tai', consisting of 150 men from the Ansar, on 100 camels and 50 horses, carrying a black banner and a white flag. They launched an attack at dawn on the encampment of the family of Hatim, Hatim al-Ta'i, the well-known Jahili figure for his generosity, demolishing Fals, plundering livestock and sheep, and capturing Adi ibn Hatim's sister, while Adi fled to Syria. (Tarikh Al-Islam, 624)
And may this present an opportunity to recount the story of Adi. Adi bin Hatim was a Christian, the son of the famously generous Hatim al-Ta'I as we said, and held in high esteem among his people. Disliking the message of the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), he left his people to join the Christians in Syria, only to find himself even more displeased there.
Abu Ubaidah bin Hudhaifah, may Allah be pleased with him, narrates the story of Adi bin Hatim, saying, "I was keen to learn about Adi bin Hatim's story, who was beside me, but I didn't approach him directly with my questions. When I finally did, he said: 'When the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, I disliked him more than anything. I fled to the farthest lands towards Syria. Then, I thought, if I were to approach this man, and if he were a liar, it would be obvious to me, and if he were truthful, I would follow him.' So, I travelled back [To Arabia]. Upon my arrival to Medina, the people exclaimed, 'Adi bin Hatim has come!'"
The Prophet (ﷺ) rejoiced at his arrival and welcomed him warmly, despite Adi's previous opposition to Muslims, his escape from battle, his disdain for Islam, and his refuge with the Christians. Yet, the Prophet (ﷺ) greeted him with a smile and led him by hand to his home.
Walking beside the Prophet (ﷺ), Adi felt as if there were no difference in their status. Muhammad (ﷺ) was a sovereign over Medina and its surroundings, while Adi ruled over the mountains of Tai and its vicinities. Muhammad (ﷺ) followed a divine religion, "Islam," and Adi adhered to another divine religion,
 
"Christianity." Muhammad (ﷺ) had a revealed book, "The Quran," and Adi had a revealed book, "The Gospel." Adi felt the only difference between them was in the intensity of power and army. However, on their way to his house, 3 incidents occurred:
As they walked, a woman stood in the middle of the road, calling out, "O Messenger of Allah, I have a need." The Prophet (ﷺ) immediately went to her, listening to her needs. Adi bin Hatim, who was acquainted with kings and ministers, watched this scene, comparing the Prophet's (ﷺ) interaction with people to what he had seen before from leaders and nobles. After deep contemplation, he declared, "By Allah, these are not the manners of kings; these are the manners of prophets."
After the woman's need was addressed, the Prophet (ﷺ) returned to Adi, and they continued their walk. Then, another man approached the Prophet (ﷺ). Did he say, "O Messenger of Allah, I have surplus wealth seeking a needy person?" Or, "I have harvested my land, and the produce is excessive. What should I do with it?" If only he had said something of the sort, Adi might have perceived the Muslims as wealthy and abundant. Instead, the man complained of poverty and destitution, barely finding food for his children, surrounded by Muslims living modestly with nothing to spare. The man spoke these words, and Adi listened. The Prophet (ﷺ) responded with a few words and moved on.
After a few steps, another man came forward, complaining about bandits, indicating the insecurity outside Medina due to enemies and thieves. The Prophet (ﷺ) addressed him and continued. Adi reflected on his position of honor among his people, free from enemies, and wondered why he should embrace a religion whose followers were in weakness, poverty, and need?
Upon reaching the Prophet's (ﷺ) house, they entered to find a single cushion. The Prophet (ﷺ) offered it to Adi as an honor for a guest, insisting he sits on it. After a brief exchange of humility, Adi sat on it. There, the Prophet (ﷺ) began to break down the barriers between Adi and Islam, urging him to embrace Islam for safety. "O Adi, embrace Islam for your safety. Embrace Islam for your safety. Embrace Islam for your safety," the Prophet (ﷺ) urged. Adi responded, "I am already committed to a religion." To this, the Prophet (ﷺ) replied, "I know more about your religion than you do." "You know more about my religion than I do?" Adi asked, puzzled. "Yes," the Prophet (ﷺ) affirmed. "Aren’t you a follower of the Rukusi faith?" This was a Christian sect with some Zoroastrian influences. Adi admitted in amazement, "Yes, that's true." The Prophet (ﷺ) then asked, "When you engage in battles alongside your people, do you partake in the division of war booty?" "Indeed," Adi conceded. The Prophet (ﷺ) pointed out, "But that is not permissible in your religion, right?" Adi felt the weight of this truth, acknowledging, "Yes."
The Prophet (ﷺ) then said, "I know what prevents you from embracing Islam. You think it's the religion of the weak and the destitute, those whom the Arabs have forsaken. O Adi, do you know of Al-Hirah [i.e., a place next to Al-Kufah, Iraq]?" the Prophet (ﷺ) inquired. "I haven't seen it but have heard of it," Adi replied. The Prophet (ﷺ) then prophesized, "By Him in whose hand is my soul, Islam will become so strong that a woman will travel from Al-Hirah to perform Tawaf around the Kaaba without needing protection from anyone. She will pass through hundreds of tribes without fear of being assaulted or robbed because Muslims will have such strength and respect that no one would dare harm a Muslim for fear of retaliation."
Upon hearing this, Adi visualized the scene in his mind, a woman traveling from Iraq to Makkah, meaning she would pass through the northern part of the Arabian Peninsula, including the mountains of Tai, his homeland. Adi was astonished and thought to himself, "What about the fierce warriors of Tai who have caused so much turmoil?"
The Prophet (ﷺ) continued, "And the treasures of Khosrow son of Hormizd will be opened to us." "Khosrow's treasures?" Adi was taken aback. "Yes, Khosrow son of Hormizd. And his wealth will be spent in the way of Allah." The Prophet (ﷺ) further foretold, "If you live long enough, you will see a man with a handful of gold or silver seeking someone to accept his charity but finding no one in need." The Prophet (ﷺ) then solemnly advised Adi about the afterlife, "A time will come when you will meet Allah with no interpreter between you. You will look to your right and see nothing but Hellfire, and to your left, again, nothing but Hellfire." Adi fell silent, deeply contemplative.
Then, the Prophet (ﷺ) challenged him, "O Adi, what prevents you from declaring, 'There is no god but Allah'? Do you know of any god greater than Allah?" At that moment, Adi declared, "I am a Hanif and a Muslim. I bear witness that there is no god, but Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and messenger." The Prophet's (ﷺ) face lit up with joy and glad tidings.
Adi bin Hatim testified, "The pilgrimage from Al-Hirah to the Kaaba without needing protection has become a reality, and I was among those who opened the treasures of Khosrow. By Him in whose hand is my soul, the third prediction will also come true because the Prophet (ﷺ) has said so." (Al-Mustadrak, modified, 4/564) (Al-Musnad, modified, No. 19378)
The conversion of Adi ibn Hatim, may Allah be pleased with him, exemplifies one of the Prophet's (ﷺ) noble characteristics: humility. This trait played a significant role in Adi's conversion. As we saw, when Adi first approached the Prophet (ﷺ) he held the perception that the Prophet (ﷺ) was either a king or a prophet. However, when he saw a weak, elderly woman stopping the Prophet for a lengthy conversation about her needs, Adi thought to himself, "By Allah, this is not the demeanor of a king." Then, observing the Prophet sitting on the ground in a humble abode devoid of royal or wealthy trappings, Adi recognized the Prophet's humility, dispelling the notion of monarchy from his mind and solidifying the image of prophethood. This serves as a lesson to all who call to Allah to embody and exhibit the trait of humility.
Humility, approachability, and gentleness were qualities that the Prophet (ﷺ) personified with both the young and old, near and far. Anyone reading his Seerah and learning of his character cannot help but fill their heart with love for him, as humans are naturally inclined to love the humble and disdain the arrogant. The stories of his humility are numerous, and his noble Seerah is replete with such instances. It is well-documented that he never behaved arrogantly towards anyone, nor did he ever boast about his status or position.
Adi's conversion also highlighted the Prophet's (ﷺ) wisdom, as he demonstrated awareness of Adi's previously held false beliefs and their contradiction. Also, the Prophet's (ﷺ) strategy in persuasion was to not merely identify Adi as a Christian but to acknowledge the specific nuances of his faith. This is akin to someone in the West today recognizing you not just as a Muslim but specifying your madhab, whether Shafi'i or Maliki, showing a deep understanding of your faith, which is a great strategy of communication. Thus, Adi became convinced of the Prophet's (ﷺ) prophethood, which knew of matters of faith unknown to others around him. After that, when the Prophet (ﷺ) perceived Adi's conviction, he spoke of barriers that prevent normal people from following the truth, even when they recognize it, such as the Muslims' weakness and their state of poverty. The Prophet (ﷺ) reassured him that security would soon prevail so that a woman could travel from Iraq to Makkah without needing protection from anyone, that the Persian Empire would fall under Muslim rule, and that wealth would become so abundant that no one would accept it. Upon the removal of these obstacles, Adi embraced Islam.
The Prophet (ﷺ) was wise in his invitation, understanding the ailments of the soul and their remedies. He tailored his call to suit the knowledge, age, intellect, status, and emotions of every individual. Thus, Adi found the signs of true prophethood in the Prophet's (ﷺ) profound wisdom and humility, just as he saw in his modest living conditions. These signs were later validated by historical events and prophecies that came to fruition after the Prophet's (ﷺ) death, further strengthening Adi's faith. Indeed, this is one of the Prophet's miracles (ﷺ), ponder on them, dear reader.
CHAPTER 14:
Appointment of Ali Over Medina:
In Rajab, the 9th year of Hijrah, the Tabuk expedition took place, which held great significance in the Prophetic Seerah and had far-reaching effects on the Muslims and Arabs, and the course of Islamic history. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) appointed Ali over Medina, providing the hypocrites an opportunity to vent their envy and hypocrisy by speaking ill of Ali, claiming his stay was due to his being a burden on the Prophet (ﷺ). This act and statement against him were clear signs of their hypocrisy, as evidenced by the authentic hadith where Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, stated: "By the One who splits the seed and created the soul, the Prophet (ﷺ) promised me that no one would love me except a believer, and no one would despise me except a hypocrite." Upon hearing their rumors, Ali took his horse and sword, caught up with the army, and expressed his desire to participate, saying, "O Messenger of Allah! You leave me with children and women?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), famously replied, as we stated before, "Are you not content to be to me as Aaron was to Moses, except that there is no prophet after me?" (Al-Bukhari, No. 2404).
CHAPTER 15:
Ali as a Missionary and Judge in Yemen:
Following the conquest of Makkah, tribes across the Arabian Peninsula embraced Islam, responding to the call of faith. The Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) dispatched missionaries to tribes that had yet to accept Islam. Among these emissaries was Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, sent to the people of Hamdan in Yemen. Al-Bara' ibn Azib, may Allah be pleased with him, narrates their journey with Ali to Yemen, saying: "When we reached the outskirts of Yemen, the news of our arrival preceded us, prompting the people to gather for him. Ali led us in the Fajr prayer, and upon completion, he aligned us into a single row before stepping forward to address the congregation. He praised Allah and recited to them the letter from the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). Consequently, the entire region of Hamdan embraced Islam in a single day. Ali wrote to the Prophet (ﷺ) about this achievement, and upon reading the letter, the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated in gratitude and said, 'Peace be upon Hamdan, peace be upon Hamdan.'" (Zad al-Ma'ad, 3/622)
After the widespread acceptance of Islam in their land, the people of Yemen required someone to educate them on the matters of their new faith, to impart knowledge, and to adjudicate among them according to the laws of Allah the Almighty. Thus, the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) sent several Sahabah to various parts of Yemen, including Muadh and Abu Musa Al-Ash'ari, among whom Ali ibn Abi Talib was distinguished for his excellence.
Thus lived Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, in close companionship with the beloved Prophet (ﷺ), drawing from his knowledge, asceticism, and noble character until the Prophet's demise (ﷺ), which nearly tore his heart apart. He had lost his beloved Prophet and messenger, his second father, who had embraced him, nurtured him, and showered him with mercy, affection, and knowledge. Moreover, the Prophet (ﷺ) had given him Fatimah, the apple of his eye and the comfort of his heart, may Allah be pleased with them all.
CHAPTER 16:
Ali in the Era of Abu Bakr:
After the death of the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), Ali remained closely associated with the Rightly Guided Caliph, Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. On the other side, Abu Bakr recognized Ali's value and status, consulting him on significant matters, often seeking his advice by saying, "Give us your opinion, O Abu Al-Hasan."
Ali, in turn, held love and respect for Abu Bakr, understanding his importance to the Muslims. A shining example of Ali's loyalty to Abu Bakr, his sincere advice for Islam and the Muslims, and his commitment to preserving the caliphate and the unity of the Muslim community was evident in his stance when Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, intended to personally proceed to the battle of Dhu Qissa and lead the military campaigns against the apostates himself, despite the risks and dangers this posed to the Islamic presence. (Al-Murtada, 97)
Therefore, Ali sent him, "I tell you what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), said on the day of Uhud: 'Sheathe your sword and do not distress us by risking yourself. Return to Medina, for by Allah, if we were to lose you, Islam would never be organized again,'" thus, he returned. (Al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya, 6/314-315)
Had Ali begrudgingly pledged allegiance to Abu Bakr, as some of the less informed claim, this would have been a golden opportunity for Ali to leave Abu Bakr to his fate, perhaps hoping for an incident to relieve him of Abu Bakr and clear the way for himself. Furthermore, had Ali harbored any ill will towards him - which is far from his noble character - he could have incited someone to assassinate Abu Bakr, as is the way of political figures with their rivals and enemies. (Al-Murtada, p. 97)
Actually, Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, advocated for battling the apostates. When Abu Bakr asked Ali, "What do you say, O Abu Al-Hasan?" Ali replied, "I say that if you leave anything taken from them by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and do not fight for it, you would be deviating from the Prophet's tradition (ﷺ)." Abu Bakr declared, "If they withhold from me even a single tether I used to receive in Zakat, I would fight them over it." (Al-Riyadh Al-Nadhirah, 670)
Ali also stated, "No one should prefer me over Abu Bakr and Umar, lest I punish them with the penalty for lying" (Fada'il al-Sahaba, 1/83).
Uqbah ibn Al-Harith said: "I went out with Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq from the Asr prayer a few days after the Prophet's death, and Ali was walking beside him. They passed by Hasan bin Ali playing with some boys. Abu Bakr picked him up and placed him on his neck, saying:
This beautiful child, in his grace *** Resembles his grandfather, the Prophet's face
Not a bit does he mirror his father Ali *** In him, the Prophet's reflection we see To this Ali laughed so hard." (Musnad Ahmad, 1/170).
Have you seen a more beautiful relationship than this among the men of Allah and His chosen ones?
Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say, "Whoever parts from the community by an inch has indeed removed the necklace of Islam from his neck" (Musannaf, 15/24).
So, would Ali do that? He, may Allah be pleased with him, detested disagreement and was keen on unity.
Al-Qurtubi said: "Whoever contemplates what transpired between Abu Bakr and Ali, from their grievances and apologies, and what it entailed in terms of agreement, would realize that each acknowledged the merit of the other, and their hearts were in agreement on respect and love. Even though human nature might sometimes prevail, the religion rectifies that, and Allah grants success." (Fath al-Bari, 7/495)
Also, Ali was among those whom Al-Siddiq consulted regarding who should assume the caliphate after him, and Ali's opinion was that it should be Al-Farooq. (Al-Kamil, 2/79)
CHAPTER 17:
Ali in the Era of Umar:
After the death of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, Umar became the Caliph and recognized Ali's worth and status. He would often seek Ali's jurisprudence, intelligence, and insight, famously saying, "If not for Ali, Umar would have perished."
Why, then, do some imagine things unsupported by true historical evidence? Ibn al-Jawzi stated that Abu Bakr and Umar would consult him, and Umar used to say, "I seek refuge with Allah from a [judiciary] dilemma that Abu al-Hasan is not present to solve." (Fadha’il Al-Sahaba, No. 1100)
One day, Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, brought forth a pregnant woman who had confessed to adultery. He decreed that she must be punished. Ali encountered her and inquired, "What is the matter with this woman?" He was told, "The Commander of the Faithful has ordered that she be punished." Ali returned to her and asked Umar, "Did you command that she be stoned?" Umar replied, "Yes, she confessed to adultery before me." Ali then said, "You have authority over her, but what authority do you have over what is in her womb?" He added, "Perhaps you scared her into confessing, or intimidated her?" Umar responded, "Indeed, that happened." Ali questioned, "Have you not heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say, 'There is no punishment for one who confesses under compulsion'? That if someone was bound, imprisoned, or threatened, then their confession is not to be accepted." Umar then released her, and thereafter remarked, "Women are incapable of giving birth to the likes of Ali ibn Abi Talib. If not for Ali, Umar would have perished" (Sunan ibn Mansour, 2/69).
It is widely transmitted that Ali, proclaimed from the pulpit in Kufa, "The best of this nation after its Prophet (ﷺ) are Abu Bakr and then Umar." This statement, as noted by Sayyid Muhibbuddin al-Khatib, is supported by more than 80 narrations recorded by Al-Bukhari and others, highlighting its authenticity unparalleled by any historical account of the prophet’s companions.
In fact, His appreciation and love for his predecessors in the caliphate were such that he named some of his sons after them. Following Hasan, Husayn, and Muhammad Ibn al-Hanafiyyah, Ali's sons were Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman. Moreover, Ali's daughter, Umm Kulthum, was married to Umar ibn al-Khattab!
“Ali supported his 3 predecessors with his advice, action, and treated them with the generosity of his conduct and speech, never showing any signs of hatred or concealed animosity. It is more fitting to say: The evidence of his loyalty during their lives and after their passing was more apparent than any signs of estrangement; for he even embraced Muhammad, the son of Abu Bakr, and provided for him, nominating him for leadership and was utterly sad when he was killed.” (Abqariyyat Al-Imam, 202)
What generation are we speaking of? Truly, it is a generation whose excellence those steeped in decline cannot even fathom, let alone reach its heights. It is a unique and distinguished generation, may Allah be pleased with them all, and may they be pleased with Him. And may the eyes of the malicious people never find rest!
Finally, to encapsulate Ali ibn Abi Talib's relationship with his predecessors without lengthiness, Al-Suyuti has relayed a saying attributed to Imam Ali, which reflects his belief that the caliphate is a right of the Ummah. The Prophet (ﷺ) passed away without appointing anyone as his successor, neither Ali nor anyone else. This also reveals Ali's support for the 3 caliphs before him and his sincere advice to them.
Al-Hasan, his son, reported: "When my father, Ali, ventured into Basra, he was approached by Ibn Al-Kawwa and Qays ibn Abbad who inquired, 'Wouldst you not disclose the nature of this expedition you have embarked upon, assuming command over the Ummah, setting some against others? Is there a mandate from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) designated unto you? Disclose unto us, for you are deemed trustworthy and veracious regarding what you have heard.'
To this, Ali responded, 'By Allah, there exists no specific mandate from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning this matter. Verily, if I were amongst the earliest believers, I would not then become the first to fabricate lies about him. Had there been such a mandate from the Prophet (ﷺ) to me, never would I have permitted my brother from Banu Taym ibn Murrah (alluding to Abu Bakr) and Umar ibn al- Khattab to ascend his pulpit (ﷺ). I would have contended against them with naught but the cloak upon my back.
But the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) departed not in haste nor did his demise come unanticipated; he endured his ailment for many days and nights. He would come forth to the believers, instructing them about the prayer, and he designated Abu Bakr to lead the people in prayer, all the while aware of my presence. Indeed, one amongst his consorts sought to divert him from Abu Bakr, yet he rebuffed and was incensed, proclaiming: 'You are akin to the companions of Joseph. Instruct Abu Bakr to lead the people in prayer, immediately.'
Upon Allah’s reclamation of His Prophet (ﷺ), we contemplated our affairs and elected for our worldly concerns the one whom the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) had sanctioned for our spiritual guidance. Prayer is the cornerstone of Islam, the pinnacle of the faith, and the edifice of belief. Thus, we pledged our allegiance to Abu Bakr, and he was deserving of such. Amongst us, there arose no dispute over this matter, we bore no witness against one another, nor was the bond of brotherhood rent asunder. I accorded Abu Bakr his due right, upheld his command, campaigned at his side, accepted his grants, engaged in battle under his banner, and enforced legal judgments with my whip at his behest.
When Umar was chosen, he followed the path laid by his predecessor, adhering to the Sunnah and established ways. Thus, did we pledge our allegiance to him, and amongst us, there was no discord. No witness stood against another, nor was the bond of brotherhood rent asunder. I accorded Umar his due respect, upheld his command, marched in his armies, fought under his command, and administered legal punishments with my whip before him.
Upon Umar's departure from this world, I pondered upon my lineage, my early embrace of Islam, my contributions, and my virtues, thinking none my equal. Yet, fearing that the one who would follow might commit deeds that would tarnish Umar's legacy, he absolved himself and his offspring from this burden. Had it been a matter of favoritism, surely his own progeny would have been preferred. Thus, he was absolved towards a gathering of Quraysh, six of us, including myself. When we convened, I thought none would outstrip me. However, Abdur Rahman bin Auf sought our vows to heed and obey whomever Allah would choose over us, then he clasped the hand of Uthman bin Affan, pledging his allegiance. Upon reflection, I realized my obedience had preceded my pledge, and my vow had been given to Ibn Affan. Hence, did we pledge allegiance to Uthman. I honored his rights, adhered to his command, fought in his campaigns, gratefully accepted his gifts, followed his orders, and carried out legal punishments with my whip in his presence.
When Uthman was martyred, I examined my position again. The two caliphs, chosen with a covenant from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding prayer, had departed this world, and this one, for whom the covenant had been made before the six, was slain; the peoples of the 2 holy cities (i.e., Makkah and Madinah) and these 2 grand cities (i.e., Kuufa and Basra) pledged their loyalty to me. Yet, one (i.e., referring to Muawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan) who was not my equal, whose kinship, knowledge, precedence, and virtues were not like mine, laid claim to it; indeed, I was more rightful to it than he is. (Tareekh Al-Khulafa’, 209-211).
And then the Fitnah (i.e., Muslims’ Civil Strife) arose between him and Muawiyah, may Allah be pleased with them both, we shall discuss it in upcoming chapters. Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: What happened between Muawiyah and Ali after the murder of Uthman, was based on ijtihad (i.e., independent reasoning) and opinion, which led to a great battle between them. The truth and correctness were with Ali, and Muawiyah is excused by the consensus of scholars, both predecessors and successors. The authentic hadiths have testified to Islam for both parties. (Al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya, 5/629)
We are certain that all Sahbah are just and that they did not covet the ephemeral world. Rather, they all sought the Face of Allah and the support of Allah's religion. May Allah be pleased with them all and gather us and them in His Paradise and abode of mercy, as brothers, facing one another in love upon thrones of happiness.
CHAPTER 18:
Ali the Leader of the Believers:
Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, was pledged allegiance to as the Caliph through a process of selection after the martyrdom of the rightly guided Caliph, Uthman ibn Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, at the hands of the insurgent rebels, the outcasts who came from various horizons and from different cities and tribes, with no previous merits or any trace of goodness in religion. It was just after they wrongfully and aggressively murdered him on a Friday, in Dhul-Hijjah, 35 AH.
All who remained in Medina from the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), pledged allegiance to Ali as the Caliph. This was because there was no one more suitable than him at that time. No one claimed the leadership for themselves after Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, and Abu Al-Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him, was not eager for it. Thus, he only accepted it after significant insistence from those Companions who remained in Medina, fearing the increase and spread of Fitnah.
Some scholars have narrated how Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, was chosen for the Caliphate:
Seif bin Umar narrated from a group of his elders: “After the assassination of Uthman, Medina remained for 5 days without a leader, with its governor, Al- Ghafiqi bin Harb, and the people searching for someone to take charge. The Egyptians were pressing Ali, who was avoiding them by hiding in his gardens, the Kufans were seeking Al-Zubair but could not find him, and the Basrans were calling for Talha who did not respond to them. They said among themselves: We will not appoint any of these three, So, they went to Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas, who was among the people of Shura, but he declined their offer. Then, they went to Ibn Umar, who categorically refused them.
