They were at a loss about what to do, then they said: If we return to our cities after killing Uthman without appointing a leader, people will be divided, and we will not be safe. So, they returned to Ali and insisted on him. Al-Ash'tar took his hand, and the people pledged allegiance to him. And they all said: No one is fit for it but Ali. When Friday came and he ascended the pulpit, those who did not pledge allegiance the day before did so. (Al-Bidayah wa-Nihayah, 10/421)
Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, Ali’s son, said: I was with my father, may Allah have mercy on him, and Uthman was besieged. A man came and said: 'The Commander of the Faithful has been killed this hour'. Ali, may Allah have mercy on him, stood up. Muhammad said: 'I held him by his waist, fearing for him'. He said: 'Let go, no mother shall be for you!' He went to the house and found the man had been killed, may Allah have mercy on him. He then went to his house, entered it, and locked his door. The people came, knocked on his door, entered upon him, and said: 'Uthman has been killed, and the people must have a leader, and we know no one more entitled to it than you. ' Ali told them: 'You do not want me, for I am better for you as a minister than a leader.' They insisted: 'By Allah, we know no one more entitled to it than you.' He said: 'If you insist, then my pledge should not be in secret. Let's go to the mosque, and there the people pledged allegiance to him.' (Al-Sunnah, Abi Baker Al-Khallel)
In another narration, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), came to him and said: 'Uthman has been killed, and the people must have an Imam. We find no one more entitled to it than you, who is senior in companionship and closer to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' Ali said: 'Do not do it, for I am a minister, better than being a leader.' They insisted: 'By Allah, we will not do otherwise until we pledge allegiance to you.' He said: 'Then, in the mosque, for my allegiance should not be hidden and must be with the consent of the Muslim.' Abdullah ibn Abbas said he was reluctant for Ali to go to the mosque, fearing disturbance, but Ali insisted on the mosque. When he entered, the Muhajirun and the Ansar came and pledged allegiance, followed by the rest of the people. (Al-Kamil Fi Al- Tareekh, 2/555)
Imam Ibn Al-Arabi affirms that none of the Sahaba abstained from pledging allegiance to Ali, even if some of them refrained from supporting him when the conflicts with the Jamal faction and with Muawiyah occurred; because pledging allegiance to him was obligatory, whereas supporting him in his war against other Muslims was a matter of ijtihad where views could differ, and perspectives vary. (Al-Awasim Mina Al-Qawasim, 300)
Hence, Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, reluctantly accepted the caliphate. He accepted it while it was a heavy burden, and a trial, just as his brothers Abu Bakr and Umar had accepted it before him, and maybe even more challenging. People came to him in distress, they flocked to him from every direction, to the extent that some of his young children were trampled underfoot, and his shoulders were split open, gathered around him like a flock of sheep, calling him to pledge allegiance, while he was shouting at them: "Leave me and seek someone else. For we are about to face matters of great concern, with various aspects and colors, hearts may not endure, and minds may not stand firm. Leadership has become obscure, and the clear path has been forsaken. If you respond to me, I will ride with you on what I know, and I will not heed the speaker's word nor the critic's reproach. And if you leave me, I am like one of you, I might listen to you and obey you more than anyone you appoint over your affairs. Indeed, I am better for you as a minister than as a leader!" (Risalah Ila Amir Al-Muminin, 43)
Thus, Ali assumed the caliphate under grim circumstances. Reluctantly, to rescue a community on the verge of unraveling. It also can be stated that Ali was the strongest candidate for the Caliphate after the death of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. Al-Farooq had appointed him among the six whom he recommended, and he was one of them. The other 4 from the council of Shurah, Abd al-Rahman, Sa'd, Talha, and al-Zubair, by renouncing their right in favor of him and Uthman, left the field open between the two. Thus, only he and Uthman remained. This was a consensus among the members of the Shurah that if not for Uthman, it would have been Ali's right. After the death of Uthman, having been preferred and deemed more deserving by the people of Medina, he became entitled to the Caliphate.
Indeed, there was no one among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), present at that time who was more entitled to the Caliphate than him, may Allah be pleased with him. He was among the first and foremost to embrace Islam, a cousin of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and his son-in-law. Besides, his capacity and competence were undeniable. He possessed courage, decisiveness, intelligence, a rare judicial mindset, firmness in positions, steadfastness in truth, and foresight in managing affairs. All these factors undeniably made him the sole candidate for the leadership of the Muslims during that critical period of their history. And despite all these qualifications, his Caliphate was legitimized after the consensus of the Muhajirun and the Ansar on him and their pledge of allegiance to him, as we reported.
CHAPTER 19:
The righteous Caliph and his lofty aspiration:
The life of Abu Al-Sibtain (i.e., Father of the two Prophet’s grandsons) and Abu Turab, Ali ibn Abi Talib, bursts with greatness, majesty, and miraculousness. From his noble self and high aspiration, expanses unfold with no bounds, sparkling with heroism, sacrifices, enormities, and glories. It almost seems, if not for the truth of history, like dreams and myths. He is a magnificent Muslim, who exudes integrity, uprightness, purity, lofty goals, and distant aims from his surroundings. A greatness that will continue to affirm itself as long as its bearer is alive, engaging in grandeur and crafting noble deeds.
He, may Allah be pleased with him, would distribute all that was in the Bayt Al- Mal (i.e., public treasury) to its rightful recipients, and when the treasury was emptied, he would order water to be brought to sprinkle the ground and wash it with water. Once this was done, he stood and prayed two sajdah on its cleansed ground!
This prayer in the public treasury, after its ground was sprinkled with water, symbolized a profound meaning, marking the new era Ali tried to build where the hereafter dominates the worldly, and piety and righteousness regain their influence over the state, society, and all souls and hearts. He was invited to descend to the Emirate's palace, a grand palace in Al-Kufah, towering in arrogance and temptation, barely seen before he turned away, saying: "This palace of folly, I shall never dwell in it as long as I live." Then, he wears a cloak bought from the market for 3 dirhams, mounts a donkey, and says: "Leave me to humble the worldly life." (Salah Al-Ummah, 67)
Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, remains a timeless figure, whose wisdom and governance continue to serve as a guide and a beacon for our era. He teaches rulers across every generation and era that allegiance to the truth necessitates the rejection of worldly temptations and the illusions of power.
Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal remarked, "The caliphate did not honor Imam Ali; rather, it was he who honored the caliphate with his magnificence.”
He wasn't graced by kingship's embrace *** But by his essence, all things find grace
Outran kings, leaving them behind *** No rival near, nor equal to find
His hands touched the highest of highs *** Beyond what vision or words can describe. (Lawama Al-Asrar Al-Bahiyyah, 2/346)
In asceticism, he soared, a heroic monk in devout worship. His greatest passion was to demean the world and its overwhelming temptations, by raising against it a steadfast and unflinching hand that declares to those temptations: No. Sufyan al-Thawri said, "He did not lay a brick upon a brick, nor a reed upon a brick; his provisions were brought to him from Medina in a sack."
He always carried his 'Dura' (i.e., Walking stick) with him through the markets, commanding the people to fear Allah and to engage in fair trade, insisting, "Give full measure and weight," and advising, "Do not puff up the meat."
One day, he went out wearing two garments, wrapped in one and draped in the other, loosening one side of his belt and tightening the other, saying, "I wear these two garments to be farther from arrogance and better in my prayer, and to set a precedent for the faithful."
Umar ibn Abdul Aziz commented, "The most ascetic of all people, without a doubt, was Ali ibn Abi Talib."
CHAPTER 20:
His Approach to Provincial Governors and His Advice to Them:
As we explained before, Ali pledged allegiance to the caliphate after the assassination of the Commander of the Faithful, Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him. The state was experiencing disturbances in various regions, placing Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, in difficult circumstances. It was a time when the Islamic state began to lose much of its stability and vitality, with the unrest clearly manifesting in Medina itself, and disturbances spreading across the state.
The advisors and counselors, sensing the gravity of the situation, came forward with advice for Ali on what could be done from the outset, especially regarding the governors of the provinces. Commander of the Faithful, Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, possessing leadership talent, understanding of people and the existing conditions, he dismissed the governors to choose others as he saw fit for achieving administrative and political harmony between the Caliph and his aides. Just as Umar dismissed some of Abu Bakr's governors, and Uthman dismissed some of Umar's, it was within Ali's right to dismiss those he believed it was in the interest to dismiss and appoint others.
It must also be noted that some contemporary critics of Islamic history have critiqued the appointment of relatives to governorships during Uthman’s and Ali’s caliphate. Uthman appointed a number of governors who were 5 from the Umayyad clan out of a total of 18 governors! When he died, only 3 Umayyads were governors: Muawiyah, Abdullah ibn Saad ibn Abi Sarh, and Abdullah ibn Amir ibn Kurayz. Therefore, we can see the exaggeration these authors are engaged in.
Then, indeed, the governors whom Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, appointed from among his relatives, proved their competence and capability in managing the affairs of their governorates. Allah granted them victory in many lands, and they ruled over the people with justice and benevolence. Among them were those who had held gubernatorial roles even before, during the reigns of Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them, such as Muawiyah, may Allah be pleased with him. Ali, followed Uthman's approach in appointing competent, capable, and righteous relatives to governorships such as his cousins Abdullah ibn Abbas, Ubaidullah ibn Abbas, Quthm and Tamam, the sons of Abbas, and Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr, his stepson.
Both Ali and Uthman appointed those whom they deemed most competent, not favoring them due to kinship. The circumstances prevailing in the governorates necessitated careful selection of governors based on strength, trust, and reliability. The frontiers, especially in the eastern provinces, were still unstable, not to mention the challenges posed by the Kharijite sects that emerged during Ali's caliphate, fighting Muslims instead of the disbelievers. (Asma' al-Matalib, Al-Sallabi, 264)
Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, diligently monitored his governors and kept track of their conditions in their governorates, inquiring about them. He employed various methods for this purpose, including dispatching inspectors to these governors to ask the people about them. Sometimes, he would have some workers inquire about others and order them to inspect their affairs. He wrote to Ka'b ibn Malik: "As for after, delegate someone over your work, and go out with a group of your companions until you pass through the land of the Sawad region to inquire about my workers and to observe their conduct." (Tarikh al-Ya'qubi, No. 28204)
Therefore, he relied on secret reports sent to him by his inspectors in these provinces, while the governors were unaware of their mission. (Al-Wilaya Ala Al- Buldan, 2/33).
These monitors could be employees of the governor or others unknown, possibly residing in the province or moving from one to another. The existence of these secret reports is evidenced by what Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, wrote to these governors. He even opened the doors wide to any complaints brought against any of his governors. When he received a complaint about one of them, he would say: "O Allah, I did not command them to oppress Your creation or to neglect Your right." (Al-Fatawa, 28, 151).
Indeed, he, may Allah be pleased with him, imprisoned one of the governors, disciplined him, and struck him with a whip upon receiving a complaint about him. (Al-Wilaya Ala Al-Buldan, 2/33)
This diligence Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, devoted to clarifying to his governors their duties, advising and guiding them according to the principles of just governance, is exemplified in the covenant he wrote for Al-Ash'tar Al- Nakha'i when he appointed him over Egypt:
"In the Name of Allah, The Most Merciful, The Most Compassionate,
Henceforth, let it not be that thy withdrawal from thy people doth extend unduly, for verily, the withdrawal of rulers from their folk doth breed distress and ignorance of state affairs. Such retreat doth sever them from understanding matters which they shun, rendering the grave trivial, the trivial grave, the fair foul, and the foul fair, intertwining truth with untruth.
A ruler is naught but a mortal; he knoweth not what his subjects conceal from him, and there exist no marks upon men to segregate honesty from deceit.
Therefore, safeguard the rights owed through the grace of approachability, for thou art one of two souls: either a soul that hath reserved its generosity, succumbing to niggardliness – then, what purpose serves thy withdrawal from a duty thou art bound to fulfill? And a virtue thou art expected to manifest?
Or a soul ensnared by stinginess and parsimony – then, how swiftly shall thy blessings flee, and how soon will the people forsake their petitions when they despair of thee? Whilst the majority of their needs require naught of thee but to lend an ear to a grievance or to mete out justice.
Thus, take heed of my counsel, confine thyself to what ensures thy well-being and piety, by the will of the Almighty.” (Al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya, 8/9)
CHAPTER 21:
A General Overview of the Nature of the Conflict:
It is universally acknowledged among historians that the conflict between Ali and Muawiyah stemmed from the assassination of Uthman. Following Uthman's murder and the allegiance sworn to Ali, a faction of the Sahabah, including Talha, Al-Zubayr, and the Mother of the Believers Aisha, may Allah be pleased with them all, believed that Ali had faltered in seeking retribution for Uthman's blood, that is, in executing the death penalty against his murderers. This belief prompted Muawiyah to withhold his allegiance from Ali and to refuse to implement his directives in the Levant.
Muawiyah contended that the Muslims should first exact the death penalty on those who killed the head of state, the third of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, before addressing the matter of the caliphate or leadership. Ali, on the other hand, maintained that his leadership had been solidified with the consensus of the Muslims present in Medina and thus was binding on all Muslims across the Islamic territories.
While Muawiyah's stance against pledging allegiance was clear, Ali considered Muawiyah and those with him from the Levant not as rejectors for a specific reason but as rebels against his authority. He interpreted their refusal as a definitive rejection of his caliphate, which was inaccurate. As the legitimate head of the state from the moment of his allegiance, he decided to subdue anyone he perceived as breaking away from his command to ensure their compliance with the Ummah's consensus.
Thus, the war between Ali and Muawiyah, the governor of the Levant, was ignited by Ali's treatment of Muawiyah as a rebel and an outsider to his authority, thereby threatening the unity of the Muslims. Muawiyah believed Ali had fallen short in fulfilling his duty of enacting the law of retribution for Uthman by killing his murderers, and his refusal to obey Ali stemmed from Ali's failure to enforce one of Allah's prescribed penalties, not just any penalty, but the law of retaliation for the murder of the most significant figure in the nation at the time, the Commander of the Faithful himself.
In other words, Muawiyah saw the execution of the law of retribution as a prerequisite to pledging allegiance to Ali, given his relation to Uthman as his next of kin. He decided to implement the law of retribution himself, although most of the assassins, or a significant number of them, were outside his jurisdiction in the Levant, being in the Hejaz and Iraq under Ali's rule. While Ali viewed this as a clear defiance of his authority and a breach of the consensus reached by the Muslims.
It is crucial to understand that Muawiyah, may Allah be pleased with him, did not wage war against Ali for the sake of claiming the authority, nor did he dispute Ali's leadership. His contention was solely about ensuring the implementation of the Islamic penal code against those involved in the assassination of Uthman, acting upon what he believed was correct, albeit his judgment in this matter was mistaken, thus he is entitled only to the reward for attempting to make a correct Islamic legal judgement. The authentic historical records clearly establish that the dispute between Muawiyah and Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, centered around the issue of avenging Uthman's murder and not over the caliphate itself, for Muawiyah acknowledged Ali's superior claim to leadership.
For instance, Abu Muslim Al-Khawlani reported that: When some people came with him to Muawiyah and asked if he was contesting Ali or considered himself similar, Muawiyah replied, "By Allah, I know he is better than me and more deserving of this affair than I am. But do you not know that Uthman was killed unjustly? I am his cousin and the seeker of his blood vengeance. Go to Ali and say that if he hands over Uthman's killers to me, I will pledge allegiance to him for the caliphate, immediately." When they conveyed this to Ali, he did not hand them over. (Siyar A'lam an-Nubala', 3/140)
Abu al-Dardaa and Abu Umamah, may Allah be pleased with them, that they entered upon Muawiyah and said to him: "O Muawiya, why do you fight this man (Ali)? By Allah, he embraced Islam before you and your father, and he is closer to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and more deserving of this matter than you." He said: "You have spoken the truth, but I fought him over the blood of Uthman, for he sheltered his killers. Go to him and say to him: 'Hand over to us the killers of Uthman, and then I will be the first to pledge allegiance to him from the people of Sham.'" (Al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya, 10/502)
These narrations and many others among the scholarly texts indicate that Muawiyah did not challenge Ali's caliphate; rather, his actions were driven by a desire to see justice served for Uthman's murder. This stance has been affirmed and clarified by scholars across Islamic history, highlighting the nuanced and principled nature of the conflicts among the Companions of the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) back at that time.
Imam Al-Haramayn states: "Even though Muawiyah fought against Ali, he did not deny his leadership, nor did he claim it for himself. Rather, he was seeking the killers of Uthman, believing he was correct, yet he was mistaken." (Luma' al- Adilla, 115)
"And it is the belief of Ahl Al-Sunna wa Al-Jama'a that the conflict which occurred between Muawiyah and Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, was not because Muawiyah contested Ali for the caliphate, due to the consensus on Ali's right to it. Thus, the Fitnah was not stirred for this reason, but it flared up because Muawiyah and those with him demanded from Ali to hand over the killers of Uthman to them, since Muawiyah was his cousin, which Ali refused." (Al- Sawa'iq al-Muhriqah, 325)
Ibn Abbas, the sage of our Ummah and its scholar, recounts: "I came to Ali after the killing of Uthman upon my return from Makkah and found Al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba - who was among the wise men of the Arabs - having a private meeting with him. After he left, I asked him, 'What did he say to you?' Ali replied, 'He came to me a few days ago and said: You have the right to obedience and counsel from me, and today's wisdom safeguards tomorrow's interests, and today's loss will be tomorrow's. So, stand up, acknowledge Muawiyah and Ibn Amir, and the governors of Uthman on their posts until their allegiance comes to you and the people settle. Then, afterwards, dismiss whoever you wish.'
Ibn Abbas asked, 'And how did you respond to him?' Ali said, 'I refused that and said I will not compromise in my religion, nor will I give in to a lower position in my command.' Ali continues referring to Al-Mughira’s statement: ‘Then, he said, 'If you refuse this request, then remove anyone you wish from the governors except Muawiya; leave him ruling over Sham, for Muawiyah has boldness and he is listened to by the people of Sham. You have a justification to keep him there since Umar bin Al-Khattab himself had appointed him over Sham and then Uthman did [for a total of 20 years].' To this, I (Ali) responded, 'No, by Allah, I will not appoint Muawiyah for even a day.' Therefore, he left me that day, and I know he wished I was mistaken. He then returned, [a few minutes ago,] and said, 'I advised you the first time with what I said, and you disagreed with it, then after that, I believe that you should do what you saw fit, so dismiss them and seek help from those you trust.'
I (Ibn Abbas) responded, 'The first time, O Commander of the Faithful, he advised you well, and the second time, he deceived you.' Ali asked, 'And why do you think he advised me?' I said, 'Because Muawiyah and his companions are worldly people and understand governance. Once they are confirmed in their positions, they do not care who holds this affair. And if you dismiss them, they will say, 'He took this affair without consultation and is sympathetic to our companion's killer,' stirring up against you until Sham and the people of Iraq revolt. Also, I do not trust Talha and Zubair not to turn against you as well [since they also seek justice for Uthman's blood with Aisha, the Mother of the Believers]. I advise you to confirm Muawiyah. Then, if he pledges allegiance, remove him from his position.'
To this Ali responded, 'By Allah, I will only give him the sword,' then he recited the poet's verse:
And death is not weakness, if its embrace I find *** No shame in it, when life's excesses leave me behind
I said, 'O Commander of the Faithful, you are a brave man, but you are not a man of strong opinion in policy of war. Have you not heard the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, say: 'War is deception.' He said, 'Yes.' I said, 'By Allah, if you obey me, I will issue them after consideration and leave them looking at the aftermath without knowing what to do, without any decrease to your status or any sin upon you.' He said: 'O cousin, I am not a man of such weaknesses, nor do I follow Muawiyah's ways in doing things.' I said, ‘Listen to me, and head to your property and lock your door on yourself. For the Arabs will never make a move and be in turmoil but will not find anyone but you. By Allah, if you stand against these people today, tomorrow people will hold you responsible for Uthman's blood.' However, no matter what I said Ali refused.
Then, he said to me, 'You advise me, and I may consider your words, but even if I disobey you, you should obey me.' I said, 'Of course, I will do that. It is the least that I can offer you, which is obedience.' He continued, 'Then, head to Sham, for I have appointed you over it.' I responded, 'This is not a wise move against Muawiya, a man from Bani Umayya, and he is Uthman's cousin and his appointee. I am not safe from him avenging Uthman's death, and at the least, he might imprison me to exert control over me due to my relation to you. And everything that is burdened upon you is burdened upon me. But write to him, then based on that, promise him.' He said, 'No, by Allah, that shall never be!'
Ibn Abbas, commenting on this story, said: “Al-Mughira used to say years later: 'I advised him (Ali), and when he did not accept my advice, I deceived him' and left for Makkah and stayed there.” (Al-Kamil Fi Al-Tareekh, 3/198)
In fairness to the truth, we must clarify why Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, requested the postponement of the punishment for Uthman's killers, which he himself explained. He said to Talha, Al-Zubayr, and the companions of the Prophet when they demanded the execution of those involved in Uthman's murder, stating that those who held Uthman's blood on their hands were in control of the people of Medina, and the people of Medina had no control over them. The slaves had turned to them, the Bedouins had sided with them, and they had power and authority in Medina, while its people could not do anything against them. Therefore, he asked the companions to wait until the situation calmed down and he could then take the criminals to account for their sins.
As for Muawiyah, the strong governor of Syria, after waiting for Ali's stance, he began to insinuate that Ali was negligent in seeking justice for Uthman's blood as we said before. He justified his accusation of Ali by his failure to execute vengeance on the insurgents. But those rebels were numerous and armed, and Ali had not yet settled into a position of authority that could support him in exacting vengeance from these thousands of armed men. However, what did Muawiyah actually do with Uthman's murderers when he came into power years later and it became his responsibility to execute the punishment for which he had stirred up conflict and sanctioned fighting? Practically, he did nothing.
The scholar Ibn Taymiyyah commented on the stance of Ali ibn Abi Talib and Muawiyah regarding the execution of Uthman’s killers, saying: "Given the division among the people, Ali was not capable of killing Uthman’s murderers without causing a Fitnah that would have worsened the situation. Choosing the lesser of two evils is preferable; because those who occupied Medina and killed Uthman were a military force supported by tribes that would be angered on their behalf. Those who carried out the murder, even if few, were backed by people of power. Without such support, they would not have succeeded in the first place. When Talha and Al-Zubayr went to Basra to seek revenge from Uthman's murderers, it led to the Battle of Al-Jamal, in which many were killed but nothing was achieved in regard to this cause.
However, after Ali's death, Muawiyah was unanimously accepted by the people as the leader of all Muslims, becoming the prince over all Muslims. Yet, even then, he did not kill those of Uthman's murderers who were still alive, due to the difficulty of doing so. If their killing was obligatory and within his power, it would have been preferable for him to act without engaging in battle against Ali and his companions for that cause. If Muawiyah had killed Uthman’s murderers, the turmoil would not have been greater than what occurred during the nights of Siffin. Therefore, if Muawiyah is excused for not killing Uthman’s murderers after becoming the caliph, either due to his inability or due to the discord and division it would cause, and the weakening of his authority, then Ali is even more excused; since the discord, division, and weakening of his authority by killing the murderers, had he pursued that, would have had a more detrimental and corrupt effect on the Ummah. (Minhaj al-Sunnah, 4/406)
Therefore, as Sheikh Ibn Taymiyyah said, after Muawiyah's situation stabilized far more than Ali's, he followed in Ali's footsteps and refused to pursue the vendetta, despite being reminded and urged to do so, but he did not change his mind. Actually, Muawiyah came to Medina for the first Hajj after the people united under him. He was met by Hasan, Husayn, and men from Quraysh. He headed towards the house of Uthman ibn Affan. As he approached the door of the house, Aisha, the daughter of Uthman, cried out and lamented her father, "Oh, my father, oh, my father."
Muawiyah told those with him: "Go back to your homes, for I have a need in this house." They left, and he entered, calmed Aisha down, ordered her to stop lamenting, and said to her: "O daughter of my brother, the people have given us authority, so we showed them forbearance under which lies anger, and they showed us obedience under which lies spite. We sold them this forbearance, and they sold us obedience. If we give them other than what they bought, they would begrudge their rights, and every person among them has a faction, ready to step up. If we break our agreement with them, they will break with us, then we do not know whether the outcome will be in our favor or against us. Being the daughter of Uthman, the deceased Commander of the Faithful, is better than being a slave among the Muslim slaves, and what a successor I am for you after your father." (Al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya, 11/433)
This illustrates how difficult it was for Ali to fulfill the condition Muawiyah and his followers wanted. Thus, Muawiyah's initial stance was not right based on all Sunni scholars’ clarifications, may Allah forgive all the companions and pardon them, Amen.
However, regarding of his stance, we remind again those who do not understand it, "He did not claim the caliphate, was not pledged allegiance to as such when he fought Ali, did not fight as a caliph, nor as one deserving of the caliphate, and everyone around him was aware of that. Muawiyah would admit this to anyone who asked him about it, and every faction among the partisans acknowledged that Muawiyah was not equal to Ali in the caliphate, nor was it permissible for him to be the caliph with the possibility of Ali's succession - for Ali's precedence, knowledge, piety, courage, and other virtues were well known and apparent to them." (Majmu' al-Fatawa, 35/ 72)
Subsequently, Muawiyah, may Allah be pleased with him, stood up to demand justice for the blood of Uthman, and he declared his willingness to enter into obedience to Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, if the penalty was enacted against Uthman's killers. If we assume that Muawiyah used the quest for retribution and vengeance for Uthman as a pretext for fighting Ali out of a desire for power, what would happen if Ali managed to enact the penalty against Uthman's killers? Surely, the result would be Muawiyah's submission to Ali and his pledge of allegiance to him, as he had committed to this stance from the beginning of the conflict. Moreover, everyone who fought alongside him did so on the basis of enacting the penalty against Uthman's killers. If Muawiyah harbored any other intentions not declared, this stance would then be a risky venture, unlikely to be undertaken if motivated by mere ambition.
Thus, it is established that no one contested Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, for the caliphate, neither those who opposed him nor others. These statements from these scholars all clarify the doctrine of Ahl Al-Sunna wa Al-Jama'ah regarding the order of the rightly guided caliphate, so it is essential to defend it, preach, educate generations upon it, and take pride and honor in associating with it.
Muawiyah, may Allah be pleased with him, was among the scribes of revelation, esteemed among the Companions, known for his truthfulness, commitment to his word, and forbearance. How could it be believed that he would fight the legitimate Caliph and shed Muslim blood for a fleeting kingdom, when he himself said, "By Allah, if I am presented with a choice between two matters, one being Allah's and the other not, I would surely choose Allah's over anything else." (Siyar A'lam al-Nubala, 3/151)
However, the mistake in his stance regarding Uthman's murder appears in his refusal to pledge allegiance to Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, before taking action against Uthman's killers, even demanding to be empowered over them, despite knowing that a blood avenger cannot judge, but should rather enter into obedience, present his claim to the ruler, and seek his rights through him.
It can be said that Muawiyah, may Allah be pleased with him, was Muta’awal acting on his interpretation, firmly believing the truth was on his side. For instance, he addressed the people of Sham after gathering them, reminding them that he was Uthman's cousin, who was wrongfully killed, and recited the verse:
{
And slay not the life which Allah hath forbidden save with right. Whoso is slain wrongfully, We have given power unto his heir, but let him not commit excess in slaying. Lo! he will be helped.
}
(Quran, 17:33) He then expressed his desire for them to pledge themselves for avenging Uthman's death, whereupon all the people of Sham stood up, responded to the call for Uthman's blood, pledged allegiance to him on this basis, and gave him their oaths and covenants to expend their lives and wealth until they avenged their cause or Allah claimed their souls. (Waqaat Siffin, 32).
So, we can clearly see here how he relied on the verse to justify his position and interpreted it in the manner we have explained in this chapter. And let us conclude this chapter by pointing to an event that summarizes the relationship between these two men.
When Dhirar ibn Damrah al-Kinani stood in the presence of Muawiyah, newly enshrined upon the caliphate in the wake of Imam Ali's demise, Muawiyah beseeched him: "Describe Ali unto me." Dhirar entreated, "Would youpermit me, O Commander of the Faithful, to abstain?" Yet Muawiyah would not grant him reprieve.
Compelled, Dhirar confessed, "By the Almighty, he bore a stature grand and a strength formidable, his words cut through doubt, his judgments bore the weight of justice. Wisdom flowed from him like a spring unceasing, and in him, knowledge found its voice. He looked upon this world and its finery with estrangement, finding solace instead in the solitude of night's embrace. By the Almighty, he was often given to deep contemplation, murmuring to the void, lost in thought. His attire incarnates modesty, his sustenance was simplicity itself. By God, he was as one amongst us; he welcomed us with open arms and addressed our queries with patience. Yet, in his presence, an awe restrained our tongues. When he smiled, it was as though pearls were strung across the room. He esteemed the devout and cherished the destitute. The powerful found no favor in injustice, the meek never despaired of his equity. I swear by Allah, I beheld him in secluded moments, under the cloak of night, the stars dimmed to his plight, swaying in his seclusion, beard in hand, writhing in an agony known only to the anguished, weeping with the sorrow of the bereft. It's as though I hear him now, plaintive in his supplication, 'O our Lord, O our Lord,' and then to the transient world he declared, 'Dost thou entice me, or pine for me? Begone, begone. Seek another's heart, for I have forsaken thee thrice, beyond which there is no return. How fleeting is thy promise, how contemptible thy companionship, how trivial thy peril. Woe, for the paucity of sustenance, the vastness of the journey, the solitude of the path.'"
Muawiyah wept then, his tears cascading down his beard, which he wiped away with his sleeve, while those gathered stifled their own sobs. He uttered, "Such was Abu al-Hasan, may Allah's mercy be upon him. And how did his loss sit with you, O Dhirar?" To which Dhirar responded, "As a mother who watches her sole child taken by the blade upon her lap, her tears endless, her heart rent in perpetual mourning." With those words, he departed, leaving the assembly in a shroud of grief. (Hilyat al-Awliya wa Tabaqat al-Asfiya, 1/58)
Therefore, let us learn from the virtues of these noble Companions who, even if there occurred among them what did occur, none of them denied the other’s rights or insulted or impugned their justice and morals. Instead, as we see here, Muawiyah was moved and perhaps knew that he was mistaken in his personal stance, and all this conflict probably would not have happened had each one fully understood the other’s position.
CHAPTER 22:
In His Chivalry and Manhood:
The etiquettes of chivalry are the key to the personality of Imam Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, from which all that is locked springs forth and all that requires explanation is elucidated. However, the etiquette of chivalry can be summarized in one word: Al-Nakhwa [i.e., Magnanimity].
Magnanimity was innate in Ali, a natural disposition he was born with, an etiquette from the noble Hashemite family upbringing, and a habit among the practical "chivalry" habits every brave knight overcoming his peers learns, even if not born into it; for the victory of the brave has a dignity that refuses to stoop to what shames and dishonors, becoming a learned magnanimity, preventing him from doing in secret what would disgrace him in public.
Thus, was Ali in all his states and actions, his magnanimity in chivalry reached its pinnacle, especially in dealing with the weak among men and women. He never ignored honor and nobility to seize an opportunity, nor did doubt in honor ever approach him. Indeed, they stand eternal as if embedded in the nature of things, so if one does what is required of him, let others forget what is required of them, even if they gained much and he suffered loss. A true knight he was, without any doubts. He faced his enemy in battle multiple times without exploiting the ripe opportunity before him; because he wished to overcome his enemy with the dignity of a noble warrior, not to prevail or exact revenge by whatever means of victory or retribution.
Among the great examples of his unique chivalric ethics is the historical incident narrated by some who witnessed the battle of Siffin between him and the army of Sham, saying: When we approached Muawiyah and the people of Sham at Siffin, we found they had chosen a flat, spacious area for themselves and took control of the water source, intending to deny us access to it.
We rushed to the Commander of the Faithful and informed him about the situation. He summoned Sasa'ah bin Sohan and said to him: Go to Muawiyah and tell him: We have embarked on this journey towards you, disliking to fight you before making a clear appeal to you, and yet you have sent your cavalry and infantry to fight us before we engaged you, initiating the conflict. We are of the opinion to refrain from you until we invite you and present our case against you. And now, you have committed another act by positioning yourselves between the people and the water, preventing the thirsty from drinking. Send a message to your companions to allow people access to the water and cease until we review what stands between us and what we have come forth for."
Muawiyah then asked his companions, and they advised him to prevent Ali and his followers from accessing the water source as an essential war tactic move. Muawiyah then sent reinforcements to guard the water and repel anyone who approached. The conflict escalated between the 2 camps with archery, spear thrusts, and sword strikes until Ali's companions broke through to the water and seized control.
At this great opportunity, had Ali willed to use it and to defeat his enemies with thirst as they had intended for him merely a few hours before, his companions came to him saying: "By Allah, we will not let them drink from it as they have denied us." Yet, Ali refused to do the same and called out to them: "Take your need from the water and return to your camp, leave them be; for Allah, the Almighty, has granted you victory over them due to their injustice and aggression."
Another opportunity had presented itself during the battle with the people of Basra, yet he refused to exploit it, angering his allies in fairness to his enemies; for he forbade them from plundering wealth and enslaving captives. They said: "Do you consider their blood lawful for us to spill but their wealth unlawful to take?" He replied: "These people are like you. Whoever overlooks our faults is from us and we are from him, and whoever resists until harmed, fighting him is upon the chest and neck."
Thus, he established for them the true tradition of chivalry or the tradition of magnanimity when he instructed them not to kill someone who turns their back, nor to finish off the wounded, nor to uncover what is concealed, nor to extend their hand to wealth. (Abqariyyat Al-Imam, 19-20).
Indeed, he was, may Allah be pleased with him, an example and a model of prophetic upbringing as a child, youth, adult, and elder. He was a miniature representation of the ethics of that lofty pinnacle known to humanity embodied in the Seal of the Prophets and their leader, Muhammad bin Abdullah (ﷺ).
CHAPTER 23:
His Gallantry in War:
As previously mentioned, a war broke out between Ali and Muawiyah, may Allah be pleased with them both, at a place called Siffin. However, we will not delve into the details of this war among Muslims, as we are already acquainted with its causes, which were based on the independent reasoning of both parties. The battle intensified, and victory leaned towards the people of Iraq and the companions of the Commander of the Faithful, Ali. Their ranks dispersed, and they were on the verge of defeat. Realizing this, they raised pieces of the Holy Quran on their spears, proclaiming, "This book is between us and you; the people are exhausted. Who will guard the borders of Sham if not the people of Sham, and who will guard the borders of Iraq if not the people of Iraq?" When the people saw the Quran being raised, they said, "We respond to the call of Allah's book and turn to it." (Tanzih Khal al-Mu'minin Muawiyah, 36)
Ultimately, this war concluded with a call to arbitrate by the book of Allah without insisting on handing over the killers of Uthman to Muawiyah or insisting on Muawiyah's allegiance to Ali and accepting the arbitration without insisting on Muawiyah's obedience to Ali. This development was imposed by the events of the Siffin War, as the war that claimed many Muslim lives highlighted a collective direction that saw the necessity of stopping the fighting and preserving blood to protect the nation's strength and maintain its power against its enemy. This is a testament to the nation's vitality, awareness, and impact on decision- making even during serious disputes. (Dirasah Fi Tarikh Al-Khilafa Al-Umawiyah, 38)
Thus, the Commander of the Faithful, Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, accepted the cessation of fighting in Siffin and agreed to arbitration, considering it a victory and returned to Kufa. He pinned hopes on arbitration to resolve the dispute, unify the ranks, and strengthen the state, aiming to resume the halted conquests.
After the end of the war rounds in Siffin, the Commander of the Faithful inspected the dead, standing over his and Muawiyah's fallen, saying: "May Allah forgive you, may Allah forgive you, for both parties" (Al-Khalifah Ali bin Abi Talib, 250).
Yazid bin Al-Asam said: When peace was made between Ali and Muawiyah, Ali walked among his dead and said: "These are in Paradise," then he went to Muawiyah's dead and said: "These too are in Paradise, and the matter is up to me and Muawiyah." (Al-Musannaf, 15/ 303).
It was also narrated that when Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, heard that 2 of his companions were publicly cursing and denouncing the people of Sham, he sent for them and told them to stop. They came and asked: "O Commander of the Faithful, aren’t we on the truth and they on falsehood?" He replied: "Yes, by the Lord of the Ka'ba, the sacred." They asked: "Then why do you prevent us from cursing and denouncing them?" He said: "I dislike for you to be people who curse; rather say: 'O Allah, safeguard our blood and their blood, reconcile between us and guide them from their misguidance so that those who are ignorant of the truth may recognize it, and those who have indulged in falsehood may desist.'" (Tahqiq Maweeqif Al-Sahabah, 2/ 232).
CHAPTER 24:
Bright Pages of His Justice:
May Allah be pleased with Abu Al-Hasan: He spoke decisively and ruled justly. His share of purity, justice, and piety was lofty and complete. His justice was towering, enduring through the ages as a beacon for the guided and the wise. His allegiance to justice was innate, a loyalty of nature and certainty.
Some of his companions reproached him for his austere life and his abstention from sufficient nourishment despite being the revered Caliph. He replied eloquently, may Allah be pleased with him: "Should I, then, rejoice in being hailed as the Commander of the Faithful, yet not partake in the common plight? By the Almighty, were I to yield to desire, I could delight in the choicest honey, the bounties of this earth, and the luxuries of garment. Yet, it is far from me to succumb, to find repose in plenty whilst around me bellies twist in famine and livers smolder in affliction.
Or as the bard once voiced:
It is a malady profound, to slumber sated *** Whilst around, livers for scraps are baited
Should it please me to bear the title, Commander of the Faithful, and yet stand aloof from the tribulations of the era, failing to embody in adversity and thrift a beacon for the flock? Not for this was I wrought, to be ensnared by feasts as beasts tethered, solely pondering their next feed, gnawing away, oblivious to a higher call. Nor was I fated to dawdle, forsaken in frivolity, led astray by the noose of folly, nor to blindly tread the mire of bewilderment.
Methinks I hear one amongst you murmur: 'If such be the lot of Ibn Abi Talib, then surely frailty hath deterred him from the clash of equals and the valor of confrontation.' Know ye, the wildwood bears the sturdiest trunk, while the garden's verdure the tenderest skin, and the desert's brush the staunchest kindle, slow to fade. Unto the Messenger of Allah, I am as kin, an arm to his shoulder. By Allah, should the Arabs conspire against me, I would not shy away. Should their throats present an opening, towards it I'd swiftly make my way. And I shall labor to cleanse the earth of every malefactor and tainted soul, until the chaff from the wheat doth part.
Turn away from me, O Dunya (i.e., Worldly Earth), for your grip loosens. I have slipped through your claws, escaped your snares, and avoided plummeting into your pitfalls. Where are the generations you deceived with your allure? Where are the nations you seduced with your glamour? They are now captives of graves and residents of tombs. By Allah, if you, O Dunya, were a visible person, a tangible entity, I would have executed upon you Allah’s Hudud for having misled His servants with false hopes, for having cast nations into abysses, for having surrendered kings to ruin, leading them to the sources of tribulation where there is neither refuge nor return.
How futile it is for one who steps upon your slippery grounds, for one who sails your tumultuous waves only to sink, and for one who veers away from your snares only to perish. And the one who is safe from you cares not if his refuge narrows, for the world to him is like the day when his soul departs. Stay away from me. By Allah, I will not be humbled by you, for you to demean me, nor will I yield to you, for you to lead me.
And by the oath of Allah, excluding His will, I shall discipline my soul rigorously, and I shall leave my eyes as if they were springs that have exhausted their tears. Shall the grazing animal fill from its pasture and then settle? Shall the fed beast satisfy from its grass and then crouch? Or shall Ali eat from his provision and then slumber? Let his eyes burst if after long years he follows the example of aimless beasts and the herded cattle.
Blessed is the soul that has fulfilled its duty to its Lord, rubbed its side with its hardship. And abandoned in the night its slumber until, when sleep overpowers, it lays on the ground and pillows its hand among those whose eyes are kept awake by the fear of their return, whose sides forsake their beds. Their lips murmur the remembrance of their Lord, and their sins are dispelled by prolonged seeking of forgiveness.
{
They are Allah's party. Lo! Is it not Allah's party who are the successful?
}
. (Quran, 58:22)" (Maarij Nahj Al-Balagha, 72)
One day, He, may Allah be pleased with him, said on the pulpit on Friday prayer: "O shepherds, indeed your flock has rights: to rule with justice, to divide with equality, and there is no good deed more beloved to Allah than a just ruler's decision" (Al-Tamhid, 2/284).
Al-Ala ibn Ammar narrated that Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, addressed the people saying: "By the one whom there is no deity but He, I have not taken from your wealth, little or much, except for this," and he brought out a vial from his shirt sleeve containing perfume, saying: "This was a gift from the Dehqan (i.e., Chef of Non-Muslim farmers community)," then he went to the public treasury and said: "Take it," then he began to say:
Blessed is he who owns a date-filled vessel *** Eating from it daily, a simple, nourishing morsel” (Al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya, 7/3)
Abdullah ibn Zarir, may Allah have mercy on him, said: I entered with Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, on the day of Eid al-Adha, and a plate of meat was brought to us, so we said: "May Allah rectify you, if only you fed us from this duck meat, for Allah has increased the good." He replied: "O son of Zarir, I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'It is not lawful for the Caliph to take from Allah's wealth but two plates: one he eats with his family, and one he feeds among the people.'" (Al-Musnad, 1/87).
Thus, piety met with justice, and how magnificent is Ali when he refrains from taking even the slightest of the nation's wealth.
Antarah Al-Shibani said: I entered upon Ali ibn Abi Talib in Al-Khurnaq wearing a cloak, so I said: "O Commander of the Faithful, Allah has allocated for you and your family a share in this wealth, how do you bear this bitter cold?!" He replied: "By Allah, I do not take anything from your wealth, and this cloak I brought from my house with." (Al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya, 11/103)
Among his acts of justice, as narrated by Ali ibn Rabia' Al-Walibi, was when Ibn al-Nabigh came to him and said, "O Commander of the Faithful, the treasury of the Muslims is filled with gold and silver." Ali exclaimed: "Allahu Akbar!!" and, leaning on Ibn Al-Nabigh, he went to the treasury and proclaimed:
This is the earth's yield, its fruit so true *** Each hand to its harvest, as destinies ensue.
[By these verses, he meant that he would not touch this money of the Muslims for himself in anyway, for it belongs to them.]
Then he said: "O Ibn Al-Nabigh, summon for me the factions of Kufa," he ordered. So, the people were called, and he distributed everything in the treasury, saying: "O gold, O silver beguile someone else." Until not a dinar nor dirham remained, then he ordered the place to be sprinkled with water, and he prayed two rak'ahs in it. (Hilyat al-Awliya', 1/81)
Ali ibn Al-Arqam reported from his father who said: "I saw Ali selling his sword in the market, saying: 'Who will buy this sword from me? By Him who splits the grain, I have long defended the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with it. Had I the price of a waist-wrapper, I would not have sold it.'" (Hilyat al-Awliya', 1/83)
And he, may Allah be pleased with him, would walk in the markets of Kufa as the Caliph of all Muslims, guiding the lost, assisting the weak, and meeting an elderly man, he would take upon himself to carry his needs. He refused to reside in the Emirate's palace, saying: "This palace of folly, I will never dwell in it."
Indeed, when we speak of the Commander of the Faithful Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, we are chronicling a legacy of human greatness and justice in its most radiant example. He taught the Ummah, saying to his soldiers: "Do not kill one who turns his back, do not finish off the wounded, do not harm women even if they insult you and your leaders, and remember Allah often so that you may succeed."
Allah blesses Abu Al-Aswad Al-Du'ali when he speaks of Ali:
Oh eye, alas, grant us solace, shed your tears *** For the Leader of The Faithful, embrace your fears
Mourn for Umm Kulthum, for him she cries *** Her tears flow, having seen the certainty that lies
Tell the Kharijites, wherever they may roam *** May the eyes of the gloating never find home
In the month of fasting, you brought us despair *** By taking the best of people, unparalleled and rare
You killed the best to mount the steeds, to tame *** And those who sailed the seas, in his name
Those who wore sandals, and those who tread *** Who recited the Quran, from it they were led
In him were all virtues, love for the Prophet's cause *** Known to Quraysh, for his lineage and his laws
And when you faced Abu Hussein's visage so bright *** You’d see the moon above, outshining the night
Before his demise, in better times we dwelt *** Seeing the Prophet’s son among us felt
He established justice, in it no doubt he held *** Fair to foes and kin, in truth he excelled
Not concealing knowledge, nor arrogance he showed *** Unlike the tyrants, in humility he glowed
As if, with Ali’s loss, people were astray *** Like ostriches in a desert, lost in dismay
Let not Muawiyah son of Sakhr gloat in vain *** For successors of the caliphs among us remain (Al-Istiiab, 3/1132)
CHAPTER 25:
The most judicious of this Ummah:
Umar ibn al-Khattab used to say: “The most judicious of us is Ali ibn Abi Talib”. And Ibn Mas'ud said: “We used to say that the most judicious of the people of Medina is Ali ibn Abi Talib. (Fadha'il Al-Sahaba, 2/699)
Abu Sa'id Al-Khudri heard Umar saying to Ali, after he asked him about something and he answered: “I seek refuge in Allah that I live in a community where you are not, O Abu Al-Hasan.” (Al-Riyadh Al-Nadhirah Fi Manaqib Al- Ashrah, 1633).
Among the tales narrated about his profound understanding, knowledge, and his judicial verdicts, there are countless instances. We have mentioned some at the beginning of this book, and here we will recount two more stories.
The first occurred when the Noble Prophet (ﷺ) sent him to Yemen. There, a lion had fallen into a pit, attracting crowds who watched, jostled, and pushed around the pit. In this commotion, one man fell into the pit and clung to another, leading to 4 men falling in and were attacked by the lion. Then, a man speared the lion to death, and the deceased were retrieved. The tribes then approached the clan of the first man who fell, arguing that his actions led to the others' deaths and demanded the blood money for the 3 deceased. The first man's clan contended they were not responsible for their fellow was also pushed by the crowd, leading to a dispute that nearly escalated to violence. A man among them cried out to Ali, who was not far from them. He, upon witnessing the turmoil among the people, approached, admonished them, and made an appeal to their sense of community, "You dare to kill each other while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is alive, and I stand among you! You may even kill people more than what is at dispute," he exclaimed. The crowd, stirred by his words, found a moment of calm.
Imam Ali then declared, "I will judge among you. If you accept my judgment, it shall stand; if not, it shall serve as a barrier until you meet the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for he is more entitled to judge than I." They agreed to his terms. He then instructed, "Gather a full, half, third, quarter of diya (i.e., blood-money) from the tribes of the people who pushed each other and witnessed the incident at the pit." The allocation was precise: "The first who fell receives a quarter of the diya, for 3 died above him. The next receives a third of the diya, for 2 died above him.
The third receives half of the diya, for 1 died above him. The fourth receives a full diya, for none perished above him." Some were content, others not, hence Ali urged, "Hold to my judgment until you meet the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who shall then decide among you."
Upon reaching the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Makkah, they relayed their story. The Prophet (ﷺ), wrapped in his cloak, announced, "By Allah, I shall judge among you." When informed of Ali's decision, the Prophet (ﷺ) inquired, "And what was that judgment?" Upon hearing the details, he affirmed, "The judgment stands as Ali decreed." Thus, the people accepted the verdict (Al-Riyadh Al- Nadhirah Fi Manaqib Al-Ashrah, 3/169).
To elucidate this matter: When the fall of these 4 was due to the crowding and jostling of onlookers, the responsibility falls upon their clans to pay the blood money for the 4 deceased. However, since the first individual was complicit in the fall and death of the other 3, his people are only liable to have a quarter of the diya. The remaining three-quarters are waived due to his role in causing the others' deaths. As for the second individual, being complicit in the fall of the other 2, the people of the onlookers are only required to pay his family a third of the diya, with two-thirds being waived due to his involvement in the death of the 2 above him. The third, having contributed to the fall of just 1 other man, his clan is liable for half the diya, with the other half waived for his part in causing the fourth's death. Meanwhile, the fourth, having no hand in causing any of the others' falls, is entitled to the full diya. From this, it is derived that these 3, each linked to the others, were neither fully autonomous in their actions nor were they completely constrained by them in a general sense.
Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, demonstrated remarkable judicial acumen and deep compassion in these narratives. In mere moments after arriving at the scene of the tragic accident, he deduced a complex judgment that the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), endorsed afterwards. This incident showcases Ali's profound understanding of Islamic Sharia and his ability to apply it with precision, intelligence, and fairness even as a young jurist.
The second narration unfolds with a man brought before Ali, when he was the Caliph, with a blood-stained knife in his hand and a corpse at his feet, soaked in blood. When questioned, he confessed, "I did it." Ali ordered, "Take him away and prepare for execution." As he was being led away, another man hurried forward, pleading, "Wait! Bring him back to Ali." So, they did.
The new man declared, "O Commander of the Faithful, it wasn't him; I am the killer." Ali turned to the first man and asked, "What made you claim to be the murderer if you were innocent?" The man replied, "O Commander, what choice did I have? The guards found me standing over the body, knife in hand, and blood on it, caught in that abandoned place. I feared my truth wouldn't be accepted, and I might be subjected to an oath, so I confessed to a crime I didn't commit, resigning my fate to God."
Ali rebuked him, "That was a terrible decision. What exactly happened?" The man explained, "I'm a butcher. Early in the morning, I went to my shop, slaughtered a cow, and was skinning it. Needing to relieve myself, I entered a nearby ruin. When I returned, intending for my shop, I stumbled upon the murder scene. Shocked, I stood there with the knife still in my hand, only to be seized by your guards." He added, “The crowd concluded, ‘He must be the murderer; who else could it be?’ Convinced that my truth wouldn't overturn their claims, I admitted to a crime I hadn't committed.”
Ali then asked the second confessor, "What about you?" The man confessed, "Seduced by greed, I killed the man for his wealth. Hearing the guards, I fled the scene and encountered the butcher, exactly as he described. I hid until the guards apprehended him and brought him to you. When you ordered his execution, I realized I'd bear the sin of his blood too, so I confessed the truth."
Ali turned to Hasan, his son who was present, and inquired, "What's the judgment here?" Hasan replied, "O Commander of the Faithful, by killing one, he has saved another. As Allah says:
{
Whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind
}
.' [Quran, 5:32] " Thus, Ali released both men and compensated the victim's family from the public treasury, after they waived their right to retribution. (Al-Turuq Al-Hukmiyya Fi-i-Siyasa Al-Shar'iyya, 36)
CHAPTER 26:
His generosity:
Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, always put others before himself, actively seeking those in need to give them from his wealth, however, he views that as a debt on himself rather than something owed to him. He said, "The noble see their good deeds as debts they must pay off, while the base sees their past acts of kindness as debts others should repay to them." Thus, he, may Allah be pleased with him, wouldn't wait for someone to ask; he himself would look for people in need from the poor, the weak, the orphans, the destitute, and give them what he believed was rightfully theirs. He once remarked, "True generosity is initiating the giving; what is given upon request is borne out of embarrassment or obligation." (Maarij Nahj Al-Balagha, 4/674)
Abu Ja'far said: Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, did not pass away until his wealth reached 100000 dirhams, mostly lands, however, he died while having a debt of 70000. Someone asked, "How did he have such debt?" People answered: His relatives and acquaintances, who had no rights for any share in the spoils, would come to him, and he would give them some money even if he did not have any. Therefore, when Hasan ibn Ali became the Caliph, he sold some of his assets and took from the edges of his wealth until he paid it off. Then, he would free 50 slaves on his behalf every year until he died. After him, Husayn continued to free 50 slaves every year until he was killed, and no one did so after them. (Makarim al-Akhlaq, 106).
It was said about him, that Abu Bakr removed the stitch of desire, and Ali tore it apart after him.
Poverty endeared to him, for in it *** Greatness found, and by such scarcity, enriched
Noble is he who leaves behind *** A legacy of honor, though wealth declined
Never did abundance in opulence rest *** For true glory in simplicity, found its nest
Wealth may crumble from its very core *** Yet, as high realms rise, it matters no more (Al-Tabsirah, 2/258)
CHAPTER 27:
His Gratitude to Allah:
It is narrated that Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, would invoke this supplication a lot, therein acknowledging Allah's blessings upon him and seeking His protection against adversities:
"All glory unto Allah, Who hath not roused me from my slumber to find myself among the deceased, nor afflicted with ailments, nor smitten upon my nape with calamity, nor ensnared by the fruits of mine own transgressions, nor severed from mine lineage, nor renounced from mine faith, nor disavowed my Lord, nor alienated from mine creed, nor befuddled in mine cognition, nor wracked with the chastisements meted unto the peoples of yore. I awakened as one under your absolute dominion, even transgressing against my very essence, with Thine argument poised against me, and none in my favor. I wield no power save that which Thou hast bestowed, and I can elude naught save that from which Thou hast shielded me.
O Allah, in Thee do I seek sanctuary, lest I find want in Thy abundance, or stray from Thy guidance, or endure tyranny under Thy sovereignty, or suffer oppression whilst the decree is Thine own. O Allah, let my soul be the foremost of the gracious boons Thou reclaimest from Thy endowments. O Allah, we seek refuge in Thee, lest we veer from Thine ordinance, or be lured from Thy true path, or our desires lead us astray absent the enlightenment bestowed by Thee. And may the blessings of Allah be upon Muhammad and his progeny." (Maarij Nahj Al-Balagha, 1/249)
He also used to say after coming out from relieving himself, while patting his stomach with his hand: "What a blessing this is, if only the servants knew how to thank it." (Uddat as-Sabirin, 122)
One day he said to a man from the people of Hamdan: " Niiam (i.e., Blessings) is tied to Shukr (i.e., Gratitude), and gratitude is linked to more. They are coupled together; thus, the increase in blessings from Allah, the Almighty, will not cease until the servant's gratitude ceases." (Al-Shukr, 11)
CHAPTER 28:
His Humility:
The humility of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him is well known, like the rest of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, may Allah be pleased with them all. He used to lie on the ground, and his body would be covered with dust. (Al-Bidaya wa'n-Nihaya, 8/6)
Saleh reported from his grandmother, who said: "I saw Ali buying dates for a dirham and carrying them in his cloak. A man said, 'O Commander of the Believers, shall we not carry it for you?' He replied, 'The head of the family is more entitled to carry it.'" (Al-Bidaya wa'n-Nihaya, 8/6)
Zadhan said: "Ali used to walk in the markets by himself while he was the Caliph, guiding those who were lost, assisting the weak. He would pass by sellers and grocers, and read [the verse]:
{
As for that Abode of the Hereafter We assign it unto those who seek not oppression in the earth, nor yet corruption. The sequel is for those who ward off (evil).
}
[Quran 28:83], and then say: 'This verse was revealed about the just and humble among the rulers, and the powerful among the people.'" (Al-Bidaya wa'n-Nihaya, 8/6)
Indeed, despite his great status and reverence, he never hesitated to show the necessary respect to those who were older than him, never forgetting their favor upon him. Suhaib, the freed slave of Al-Abbas, said: "I saw Ali kissing the hand and foot of his uncle Al-Abbas and saying: 'O uncle, please be pleased with me.'" (Al-Dhahabi in Siyar A'lam an-Nubala', 2/94)
CHAPTER 29:
His Asceticism:
We have mentioned many instances throughout this book that demonstrate the immense asceticism of Imam Ali, however, we will dedicate this entire chapter to illustrate more aspects of his asceticism. He was pleased with coarse clothing and rough living. And by saying "he was pleased," we do not mean the pleasure of love but the commitment to despising this worldly life to the utmost extent.
He would stand at night when the darkness enveloped and the stars dimmed, in his prayer niche, clutching his beard, writhing in the agony of the pious, and weeping the tears of the sorrowful, saying: "O Dunya, have you displayed yourself to me? Or longed for me? Away from me, deceive someone else. I have divorced you thrice; there is no returning for me to you. Your duration is short, your worth is little, and your danger is great. Oh, may God help me regarding the scarcity of provision, the length of the journey, and the loneliness of the road."
Hisham ibn Hasan said: While we were with Hasan Al-Basri, a man from Al- Azariqa, a faction of the Kharijites whom Ali had fought before, came asking: "O Abu Said, what do you say about Ali ibn Abi Talib?" Al-Hasan's cheeks turned red in anger as he said: "May Allah have mercy on Ali. Indeed, Ali was a precise arrow of Allah against His enemies and stood at the noblest and closest station to Allah's Messenger, (ﷺ). Truly, he was the monk of this nation, not inclined towards worldly possessions, nor neglectful in the matters of Allah. He gave the Quran its due in decrees, deeds, and knowledge, thus flourishing in verdant gardens and clear signs. That is Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib, oh ignorant fool one."
Zaid ibn Wahb said: A delegation from the people of Basra came to Ali, among them was a leader of the Kharijites named Al-Ja'd ibn Ba’aja. He addressed the people, praising Allah, and then said: "O Ali, fear Allah, for you will die, and you know the way of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him." Ali replied: "By the One in whose hand is my soul, rather by being killed, a strike on this [pointing to his beard] will stain this [his head] with its blood, a decreed fate and a promised covenant. And he who fabricates has failed." He then reproached him for his worn-out clothing, asking, "What prevents you from wearing fine garments?" Ali replied: "What concern is my clothing to you? It keeps me from feeling arrogance and is more likely to be emulated by Muslims." (Az-Zuhd, 1/109)
Ali was once presented with Faloodeh (i.e., a type of Persian sweet), placed before him, he remarked: "You smell pleasant, look beautiful, and taste delicious, but I dislike accustoming myself to what I'm not used to," then he discarded it. (Az-Zuhd, 1/109)
CHAPTER 30:
Golden Words:
Herein lies a fragrant bouquet of his words, may Allah be pleased with him, that ought to be engraved in gold on the pages of our hearts:
Waki' narrated that Ali ibn Abi Talib said: "Seek ye knowledge that by it, ye may be renowned, and act so thou mayest be counted amongst its folk. For lo, a time shall come upon thee when truth, in nine parts of ten, shall be refused, and none shall escape save those repentant and devout. They are the beacons of virtue, the bearers of wisdom, not given to rashness nor to sowing seeds in haste."
And he spoke thus: "Lo, the world hath turned its back, departing, whilst the Hereafter draws nigh, advancing. Each claims its progeny, so choose ye to be offspring of the Hereafter, not of this fleeting realm. For those who forsake worldly allure have claimed the earth as their tapestry, the soil as their couch, and pure water as their scent. Verily, he who yearneth for the life to come shall shun desire, and he who feareth Jahannam shall eschew forbidden acts, and he who seeketh Jannah shall hasten towards acts of obedience, and he who relinquisheth worldly attachment shall deem trials but trifles.
Indeed, to Allah belong servants as if they see the people of Jannah in Jannah, dwelling forever, and the people of Jahannam in Jahannam, tormented. Their evils are avoided, their hearts are sorrowful, their selves are chaste, and their needs are light. They endured a brief hardship for long-lasting comfort. As for the night, they stand in vigil, their tears streaming down their cheeks, imploring Allah for the salvation of their necks. And during the day, they are thirsty, patient, virtuous, and God-fearing, as if they are the unstruck arrows; when looked upon, the observer says they are ill, yet there is no illness in them, and they are deeply affected, indeed, they have encountered something profound." (Al-Bidaya wa'n-Nihaya 8/8)
Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "In this mortal realm, men dost be divided into 3 sorts: one, a divine scholar, bathed in Heaven's light; the next, a seeker, treading the path toward redemption's gate; and last, the heedless throng, that followeth every clamor loud, tossed by every tempest's blow, unlit by wisdom's glow, nor anchored to a steadfast hold. Verily, knowledge dost outweigh wealth. For knowledge doth thy guardian be, whilst thou must need safeguard thy wealth. In deeds of goodness, knowledge grows, but wealth by spending lessens so. To love a scholar is to worship's height aspire. His wisdom commands respect whilst he yet breathes, and in death, a fond remembrance keeps. Yet wealth, once spent, doth vanish into naught. The hoarders of riches find death in life's embrace, but scholars through the ages span; though flesh may fade, their teachings in the heart remain, a beacon bright across the darkened spans of time. (Al-Bidaya wa'n-Nihaya 8/6)
And he, may Allah be pleased with him, also said: "That which I dread most for thee is twofold: the pursuit of whims and the stretching of aspirations. Pursuing whims veers one from verity's path, whilst the lengthening of aspirations makes one oblivious of the life to come. Lo, the mortal realm hath turned its visage away, retreating, and the life hereafter draweth nigh, each claiming its progeny. Be thou amongst the offspring of the hereafter, not of this transient world, for today deeds are wrought sans reckoning, and on the morrow reckoning comes, bereft of the chance for deeds." (Al-Bidaya wa'n-Nihaya, 8/8).
And he, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Be ye fountains of erudition, repositories of sagacity, beacons in the gloom, cleansers of the spirit, rejuvenators of hearts, renowned in the celestial, concealed upon the earth, remembered by your Lord. Verily, the consummate scholar is he who leads not the masses to despair of Allah's grace, nor assures them of immunity from Allah's wrath, grants no license to trespass against Allah, forsakes not the Quran for aught else. Naught of worth lies in devotion devoid of lore, nor in learning absent comprehension, nor in perusal lacking reflection. It is not in wealth nor progeny that the world's worth is found, but in the abundance of knowledge, the nobility of patience, and in the pride of servitude unto your Lord. When ye act rightly, praise be to Allah; when ye err, seek His forgiveness. And naught of value doth this Dunya hold save for twain: one who errs and mends with penitence, and one who vies in virtuous acts, aspiring to loftier stations.” (Al-Bidaya wa'n- Nihaya 8/9)
In another narration, Abu Araka recount: “I attended the Fajr prayer with Ali, and after its conclusion, he sat in solemnity till the sun ascended a spear's height above the mosque's enclosure, then he turned his palm skyward and avowed: "By Allah, I have beheld the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), yet today I see naught that mirrors them. They greeted dawn with pallor, disheveled, dust-enrobed, bearing marks upon their limbs like the joints of camels from prolonged genuflections, night spent in worship and Quranic recitation. In remembrance of Allah, they swayed as trees do on tempestuous days, their eyes weeping till their cloaks were drenched. By Allah, it seems as though the folk have lapsed into heedlessness." Then he stood up and was never seen laughing freely again until he was struck by Ibn Muljam, the enemy of Allah, the wicked." (Al-Bidaya wa'n-Nihaya 8/7)
Al-Asbagh ibn Nabatah recounted that Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah's favor rest upon him, once mounted the pulpit. Having extolled Allah and spoken of the inevitability of death, he proclaimed, "O ye servants of Allah, death is but an unyielding certainty. Whether ye hold fast or flee, it shall surely claim thee. Thus, in preparation lies thy salvation, and woe unto those who tarry. For lo, behind thee pursues the grave; beware its suffocation, its gloom, and its isolation.
Take heed, for the grave doth thrice daily proclaim, 'I am the abode of gloom, I am the abode of vermin, I am the abode of solitude.' Beware, for beyond this awaits a day when youth shall gray, and the elders shall falter,
{
Every nursing mother will forget her nursling and every pregnant one will be delivered of her burden, and thou (Muhammad) (ﷺ) wilt see mankind as drunken, yet they will not be drunken, but the Doom of Allah will be strong (upon them).
}
(Quran, 22: 2) And verily, that which follows is yet more grave: a blaze of fierce heat, of profound depths, with shackles and flails forged of iron, where the draught is pus, and its custodian is Malik, upon whom descends not Allah's grace."
Then he wept, and those amongst the faithful who surrounded him wept as well. Continuing, he uttered, "Yet beyond lies Paradise, vast as the skies and the earth, readied for the virtuous. May Allah count us and you amongst the virtuous and shield us and you from the grievous torment.
He elaborated further, "The world recedes, signaling its departure, whilst the Hereafter draws nigh and looms vast. This day is for preparation, and the morrow for the race. Verily, you dwell in days of aspiration, succeeded by the moment of destiny. He who lags in his days of aspiration ere his moment of destiny arrives, his deeds shall fail him. Strive in the cause of Allah with earnestness as ye strive with fear. Verily, I have not beheld the likes of Paradise where its seeker slumbers, nor of hell where its fleer rests. He who is not fortified by truth shall be undone by falsehood, and he who is not steered by guidance shall be misled into straying. Ye are bid to venture forth, and light hath been made your provision.
O folk, this world is naught but a transient delight partaken by both the righteous and the wicked, while the Hereafter is a veritable promise, governed by a potent Sovereign. Indeed, Satan entices you towards penury and bids you to foul deeds, whereas Allah promises you forgiveness from His bounty and abundance. Allah is all-encompassing, all-knowing.
O folk, hasten in your earthly span to safeguard your eternity. Allah hath pledged His Paradise to those who heed Him, and warned of His Fire to those who defy Him. It is a fire whose bellow ceases not, whose captives find no release, whose shattered find no repair. Its heat is fierce, its depth immense, and its draught is pus. And what I dread most for you is the pursuit of desires and the elongation of aspirations." (Al-Bidaya wa'n-Nihaya 8/8)
CHAPTER 31:
A Profound Sermon:
Ja'far ibn Muhammad reported that Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, followed a funeral procession. When the deceased was placed in the grave, and his family wailed and wept for him, he said: "Why do you weep? By Allah, if they could witness what their deceased is facing, their own sight would distract them from their grief for him. Indeed, the Angel of Death will return to them until none remains.
He then stood and said: "I exhort thee, O ye servants of the Almighty, to revere Allah, who hath set forth parables for your edification, determined your destinies, and bestowed upon you ears that hearken, eyes that perceive, and hearts that understand. Verily, Allah hath not wrought you in jest, nor hath He forsaken your mention. Nay, He hath ennobled you with copious blessings and arrayed for you a recompense. So, fear Allah, O servants of the Most High, strive with earnestness, and make haste to act ere the spoiler of delights doth overtake thee. For the comforts of this world endure not, nor are its tribulations to be deemed reliable. It is but a deceiving adornment and a faltering support. Heed, O servants of Allah, the lessons imparted.
Let warnings admonish thee and gain wisdom from the exhortations, for verily, it is as if the talons of death have ensnared thee, thou art destined for the soil, and the harrowing events have befallen thee with the sounding of the Trumpet (Israfil’s), the scattering of graves, the gathering on the Day of Resurrection, and the reckoning, all within the dominion of the Omnipotent. Every soul is driven unto its gathering, and a witness testifies over it. The earth shall be aglow with the light of its Lord, the record laid bare, the prophets and witnesses summoned, and judgment rendered in truth, and none shall be wronged. Thus, shall the earthquake on that day, the herald shall proclaim, the beasts gathered, secrets unveiled, hearts quake, and Hell brought forth, its flames intensified, and its scalding waters magnified.
